entry.title: Advantage, Evenepoel? The Tour de France 2027 route attempts to stop the inevitable
entry.content:
Cyclist
Advantage, Evenepoel? The Tour de France 2027 route attempts to stop the inevitable

After rumours, speculation and sleuthing, the parcours for the 2027 Tour de France was finally revealed in Paris yesterday in front of an audience that included former Tour winners, legends and esteemed local politicians.

Starting in Scotland on 2nd July 2027, the race will spend three days in Britain before heading to France, where the GC will rip open. In total, next year’s Tour will feature seven sprint stages, six hill stages, six mountain stages and 71km of time-trialling. Between those numbers lies our first clues of where the GC could be won or lost, and who the route designers seemed to have favoured going into the 2027 edition.

It’s clearly been a tough ask to create a Tour that avoids a certain Slovenian from ending up with a bucket full of stage wins and building a winning advantage so large it looks like a timing error. But have Thierry Gouvenou and his band of merry men made any inroads into hampering Tadej Pogačar in 2027? Who has this course been created to benefit?

Who would the race organisers be considering?

How do you stop a five-time Tour de France winner from what seems like an unchallenged sixth win? Not much, but you can try to help out the challengers.

Jonas Vingegaard has been the runner-up to Pogačar on three occasions. The Dane was once said to be stronger on pure mountain stages, which perhaps motivated the mountain-heavy course in 2024 and 2025. That has since been dispelled, and now he just seems to be a bracket behind Pogačar in the mountains. He doesn’t seem to have the time-trial legs to set him apart, neither is he a gifted enough puncheur to warrant several steep finishes in his name.

Instead, the Tour could look to Remco Evenepoel as the possible challenger – or at least the man to suspend Pogačar’s yellow jersey tyranny. The Belgian finished last year’s Tour over six minutes behind Pogačar, but the Red Bull rider seems to be growing in confidence and strength. Physiologically, he should be entering his best years too, as he turns 27 in January. He also has a distinct advantage, being the world’s best time-trialist.

Then there’s Paul Seixas. It’s no secret that Gouvenou has tried to design routes that favour certain French riders in the past. Particularly in the age of Thibaut Pinot and Romain Bardet’s peak, the Tour’s route map seemed to favour the pair – the race even visited both of their hometowns in 2019 and 2020.

But how can you tailor a Grand Tour to Seixas? It’s not clear yet. He seems to thrive on punchy parcours, but so does Pogačar. So at this point in time, you can’t hand Seixas a huge advantage – besides visiting his hometown (which won’t happen in 2027).

Historic levels of time-trialling

A noticeable feature of this Tour de France is the whopping 71km against the clock. The Tour de France hasn’t featured this much time-trialling since 2012, the year they whacked in a bunch of kilometres against the clock in the favour of Bradley Wiggins – around 100km on that occasion.

The only domain Pogačar has genuinely felt behind his rivals is in the time-trials. That reason has no doubt motivated the big shift toward adding time-trials into the race, notably in the favour of Remco Evenepoel, a four-time world champion in the discipline.

The Belgian’s team have already clocked onto this assumption.

‘It’s not bad at all for us,’ Red Bull boss Ralph Denk said after the route presentation yesterday. ‘Remco is currently the very best time trialist in the world, so that is an aspect of this Tour we are certainly going to take into account. That he can gain time on Pogačar, Vingegaard, Seixas and co in those? In theory, yes.’

His confidence is justified. Evenepoel has won three of the five time-trials he has ridden at the Tour. The only ones he missed were considerably uphill, favouring stage winner Tadej Pogačar instead.

Given the addition of a huge 38km flat time-trial on Stage 7, Evenepoel has been touted as the first serious yellow jersey wearer. Judging from recent performances, he has been handed the chance to make early inroads on Pogačar, potentially setting him up for a several-day stint in the race lead.

For those tired of seeing Pogačar take yellow early, this would be an improvement. Plus, it would at least give the illusion that the race is more undecided than it was in previous years when Pogačar went into the jersey with ease during week one.

The time-trial in Toulouse could also fling Evenepoel closer to the GC lead if he is to lose it in the Alps. Again, it’s over 30km in length, so there’s a chance for another 30 seconds to be picked up here. Combined, you could guesstimate that a total of 1 minute to 1 minute 30 seconds could be gained by Evenepoel in these two stages alone.

There is an important caveat to be made here.

We are assuming that Evenepoel will be much stronger, and thus, will gain a handsome amount of time. This is founded on his results at championship races like the Worlds, Olympics and Europeans. But when Evenepoel and Pogačar have gone head-to-head against the clock at the Tour, the gaps have been tighter than you might have thought.

In a 33km flat TT in the first week of the 2025 Tour, Evenepoel gained just 16 seconds on Pogačar. In a 25km stage the year before, he gained just 12. Sure enough, he gained 28 seconds on a 26km course in 2026, but these gaps are far from the minute-or-so margins we see him winning by at the Worlds.

Based on average speeds and time gaps, the maths suggests Evenepoel may only stand to gain around one minute from these 71km against the clock. That’s if our sample of previous Tour performances is to be believed.

That’s hardly an open goal when you’re up against Pogačar, but it definitely hands Evenepoel a leg-up in his GC quest.

Fewer mountaintop finishes

While time-trialling is in, summit finishes are out.

In 2027, the organisers have included only three finishes atop mountain passes. That’s the lowest figure since 2017, when the Tour tried their best to stunt the ‘Sky Train’ and natural climber Chris Froome. To some extent, it feels as though the same tactic is being employed here against Pogačar, who has seemed near unstoppable in the mountains over the past few editions, having developed a successful copy-paste approach to these types of finishes.

On closer inspection, it looks like the route is trying to avoid big mountain days in general, particularly within the race’s opening week. It’s a logical approach after recent editions at which Pogačar has forced race-deciding results in the mountains early on.

That fear might have tempered the route organisers from delivering a blockbuster mountain stages filled with hors catégorie climbs after hors catégorie climb. Instead, the mountain profiles look tamer than in previous years. The thinking goes that this approach should limit the opportunities for big GC gaps to be created, as riders will have more teammates at their disposal and less mountain fatigue in the legs.

The stages in the Alps are noticeably less extreme than 2024, 2025 and 2026, when the riders would be served at least one stage with over 5,000m of elevation gain. In 2027, we have nothing of the sort. The stage to Sallanches ends with shorter climbs, while the stage to Les Saisies limits the usage of monster climbs before the final test.

In fact, the length and altitude of many of the climbs selected seem to be much tamer. The Tour’s highest point will be the lowest it’s been since 2013, and the longest climb of the race is just 20km. These stages are shorter than before too, with few mountain days set to be above 170km.

I guess that’s one way to stunt Pogačar. Take out the mountains because he’s too good at them.

That approach, however, should place extra emphasis on GC gains elsewhere, notably the time-trials. And while Evenepoel might have won his first mountaintop finish at the Tour this summer, he’s not the most gifted on these blockbuster days in the Alps. A move away from summit finishes, where the climbing is the ultimate variable, could therefore be seen as something else in his favour.

It’s impossible to Pog-proof a Tour

While the Tour has done its best to give Evenepoel a leg-up and deter fatal Pogcineration before the end of week one, the race can’t protect itself too much from what has felt like an inevitability for the past few years.

Let’s face it, it’s impossible to make a route that hampers Tadej Pogačar. He’s proven that he can take time on any and all terrain, from cobbled to time-trials, hills and Pyrenean passes. He also has the world’s best team at his disposal and a pre-Tour programme that is well-proven for French success.

However, what we have learnt is that placing the mountains early on is a risk. When before it added a light dusting of GC intrigue, Pogačar has taken the opportunity to strangle the race early on. That’s been noted this year, and the mountain stages have been made much easier than in previous years. The placement of the time-trials also feels like a wise choice, giving purists like Evenepoel somewhat of a GC handicap coming into the Alps and Pyrenees.

Pogačar will probably end up winning the Tour in 2027. But we just might have to wait until week two for him to take yellow and start putting minutes into his rivals. That’ll be an improvement at least on the 2021, 2024, 2025 and 2026 editions, when Pogačar seemed the winner-in-waiting already by the end of week one.

In an age of five-minute winning margins and two-week stints in yellow, something needs to be done to change the current course of action. If long time-trials are the answer to that – and I believe they could be as long as Evenepoel remains a contender – then so be it. Let’s throw them in and make the Tour feel more up in the air, even if it isn’t really.

Picture this. Evenepoel ends up in the yellow jersey after Stage 7, picks up a lead of maybe one minute, just to be dumped once the race reaches the Alps. We’ll get a second wind of optimism after the second time-trial, only for it to disappear once Pogačar reminds us of what dominance looks like in the Pyrenees. The outcome is the same, but the journey there has been engineered differently to the five Tour wins before.

In that case, Remco, I am afraid you are ASO’s Trojan Horse.

The post Advantage, Evenepoel? The Tour de France 2027 route attempts to stop the inevitable appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Winners and losers of the 2027 Tour de France route
entry.content:
Cyclist
Winners and losers of the 2027 Tour de France route

It’s time to get your calendars at the ready because the 2027 Tour de France route is finally out in the open.

Get the macaroni pies and Buckie while you’re at it because the 114th edition will begin in Scotland for the first time, with a send-off scheduled in Edinburgh on Friday 2nd July 2027. From there, the route cuts down through England and Wales before meeting the race’s homeland, where the fight for the yellow jersey will no doubt take shape. The Grand Colombier, Col du Portet and Col de Marie Blanque are among the big mountain passes to feature, but all the talk after yesterday’s route reveal seems to be centred on the 71km of time-trialing sprinkled into the first and final week of racing.

So, what are the takeaways from this parcours reveal? Who looks to benefit the most, and who is already booking their flight to Italy after seeing next year’s Tour route for the first time?

Winner: Remco Evenepoel

After finishing second at the 2026 Tour de France, Evenepoel has been considered to be Tadej Pogačar’s closest threat.

This can be seen in the parcours, which features 71km of individual time-trials, the largest sum in 15 years. That should be enough to not only guarantee the four-time world champion’s participation, but also secure him as a shoo-in for the final podium.

Along with the potential for two stage wins, Evenepoel has the chance to gain yellow after Stage 7’s time-trial to Chambord. It’s an open goal wider than the English Channel, and as long as he stays close enough to Pogačar in the Welsh hills, the Belgian will be in prime position to take the maillot jaune.

If he moves into yellow, Evenepoel could end up leading the race for a few days. The position of the second time-trial before the Pyrenees could also slot him into a healthy GC position coming into the final mountain stage. Given he’s never worn yellow before, I presume he’ll be sure to seize the moment when it comes next July, potentially handing us our first genuine challenger to Pogačar in several years.

Winners: The sprinters

The 2027 Tour de France will give the sprinters much to think about.

The chance to fight for the yellow jersey comes early on, not once but twice on British roads.

This is because Stage 1 looks to be a sprint-friendly finale, albeit with a false flat arrival in Carlisle, while Stage 2 looks to favour the sprinters again by Liverpool’s Pier Head. So if you don’t manage to get yellow on day one, you can always pick it up after Stage 2 if the bonus seconds are on your side. In that case, we could have the rare chance that two sprinters end up in yellow during the Grand Départ.

The green jersey battle was by far the most compelling contest to follow at the 2026 Tour. However, the way in which it was fought was somewhat atypical, with riders heading off into the breakaway instead of relying on sprint results. The outcome was a green jersey winner, Mads Pedersen, who failed to crack the top five in a bunch sprint.

On the whole, I’d say the 2027 route leans more toward the traditional sprinters, given there are seven flat stages. Many of them come early on, so there’s an even higher chance of them ending in a sprint and thus the green jersey points going toward a traditional sprinter instead of a fast rouleur like 2026 green jersey winner Mads Pedersen.

I say this, but Tim Merlier has already said that he’s going to the Tour solely to win stages instead of fighting for the green jersey. The sprinting field is also more fragmented than ever, evidenced by the fact that four different sprinters won stages at the 2026 edition.

Winner: Mathieu van der Poel

The Tour de France route designers have every reason to give Mathieu van der Poel a leg-up. He’s hugely popular domestically and abroad, and he has a star quality that seems to transcend the sport’s usual borders.

In that case, it’s not shocking to see several Van der Poel-friendly profiles in week one. In particular, there are a pair of finishes that come back-to-back on Stages 4 and 5. The finish to Cherbourg was last used in 2016, when a reduced group made it to the line. Watching that stage back reinforced my belief that Van der Poel could be in with a shout there. That’s the same for Stage 5’s finish to Plumelec, which boasts similar stats to the Mûr-de-Bretagne, where he won his first Tour stage back in 2021. It’s worth remembering that Marianne Vos won on the same climb when the Tour de France Femmes visited last year, and we all know the similarities the two Dutch riders share.

If he’s brushed up his climbing legs, as he did in preparation for the Worlds in Montréal last month, then he could even be in with a chance for a stage win and yellow jersey in Cardiff. He’s a former winner of the Tour of Britain, after all.

Winners: Polka-dot purists

All too often we have seen the winner of the Tour de France end up in the polka-dot jersey without even trying. It happened in 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2025, when either Jonas Vingegaard or Tadej Pogačar won the polka-dots without ever wearing it on the road.

However, the 2027 Tour de France will feature just three summit finishes. That’s the smallest number of mountaintop finishes since 2017, when the Tour de France removed the prospect of endless Chris Froome victories in the mountains.

A byproduct of this summit finish shrinkage could be a return to proceedings for the polka-dot jersey. The GC monopoly in the mountains classification has typically been a result of the summit finishes, which yield high returns in the fight for the polka-dot jersey. If you remove the opportunities for Pogačar and Vingegaard to score points, the traditional breakaway candidates gain an advantage.

Another advantage of this route is the early placement of several key mountains. On the stages to Sallanches, Mende and Laruns, the breakaway should have free rein to contest the bulk of the day’s points. That should favour their chances in the overall contest rather than having UAE and Visma domestiques rake in the points by default.

Loser: Lenny Martinez

The race organisers have often been accused of creating routes that favour French riders. However, those accusations fall short when discussing Lenny Martinez – who finished fifth at this year’s race, don’t forget.

Why is this parcours unfavourable for him? Well, he’s far from a natural on the TT bike. At this year’s Tour, he shed almost three minutes in the 26km time-trial. In a Tour with over double that, we could see Martinez struggle to replicate his top five finish next July.

To add insult to injury, Martinez won’t benefit from a parcours littered with summit finishes either, his usual terrain for success.

If I were him, I’d go for the polka-dots instead of a top ten overall. Just don’t go grabbing any sticky bottles this time, Lenny.

Losers: Anyone who thrives at high altitude

Sorry to all the riders born in the Andes or Rockies. This Tour is not going to give the high-altitude babies any advantage. In fact, the Tour only passes the 2,000m marker on one stage, Stage 18.

This is the lowest-altitude Tour de France in a long time – and that’s judged by several metrics. The 2,115m summit of the Col du Portet is the lowest highest point used since the 2013 Tour de France. The 2027 race only goes above 800m altitude on six occasions. So if anyone was planning on acclimatising to 2,000m altitudes, it’s not worth bothering.

We used to talk about how Colombians thrived on high-altitude finishes, but perhaps that line of thinking is démodé in an age where riders born in Scandinavia and Benelux climb among the best in the world. 2,000m also insinuates longer climbs. If that means more space for Pogcineration, the less the better.

Losers: Weekend viewers

There are a few confusing choices at this Tour de France – and I’m not talking about the choice to send the riders to deepest, darkest Cardiff.

Weekend viewership is almost always higher than it is during the week. That’s the race’s chance to get the race on more eyes, and potentially capture new audiences channel hopping on a Saturday or Sunday afternoon. In that regard, it should be in the race’s best interest to have exciting stages on Saturdays and Sundays, of which there are eight at next year’s Tour.

Fair enough, the opening weekend will attract viewers regardless, but there are two sprint stages scheduled for the second and third weekends. For new viewers, the prospect of seeing the peloton roll as one big blob will probably look rather boring. Not to mention the lack of jeopardy these stages hold in the GC.

The final weekend is a particularly lucrative window for viewership ratings. The Montmartre finish has helped to increase viewing figures in France, as revealed during the route presentation yesterday, but the decision to make Stage 20 a transitional stage feels rather silly. Chances are, the stage will be fought out by a fatigued breakaway or a peloton just wanting the race to be done and dusted. I mean, the same happened in 2025, when a slightly more interesting profile was chucked in to keep the Ain and Doubs départements happy.

I understand the choice to minimise transfers to Paris – especially after the Tour committed to using rail instead of flying domestically – but Stage 20 should be a GC showpiece. Why not move the route around to have the final Pyrenean stage then?

Losers: Tougher sprinters

While sprinters like Tim Merlier and Olav Kooij have a right to be happy about this route, there are few reasons for the likes of Mads Pedersen and Biniam Girmay to feel overlooked. Similarly, it’s hard to see the likes of Paul Magnier or Arnaud De Lie having a breakthrough Tour de France either.

That’s because there aren’t many stages suited to a reduced bunch sprint, or any that suit a tougher sprinter of the Pedersen type. The finish to Cherbourg could prove too steep, as is the finish up to Plumelec upon the race’s return to France. A lot of the early chances for the fast men look like out-and-out sprints. The hillier stages, on the other hand, look too difficult for a sprinter to get their hands on victory.

If you’re Pedersen or Girmay, the most appetising profile is Stage 15 to Albi. With it coming so deep into the race though, it’s likely a breakaway ends up contesting the win anyway. Knowing Pedersen, he’ll try his damn hardest to get into the day’s escape group, however.

Losers: Fans wanting to go to the Team Presentation

This one isn’t quite related to what we heard yesterday morning, but rather the events around the Grand Départ.

This morning, tickets went on sale for the Team Presentation of next summer’s Tour de France, which is set to take place just outside Edinburgh Castle. The setup will feature a stadium-like setup – just like the Edinburgh Tattoo – instead of the usual town square rig that the Team Presentation has adopted in previous years.

Tickets started from £27, but the pre-sale already sold out this morning due to high demand. More tickets are due to go on sale next week, but I have certain reservations about this approach.

I say the fans in Edinburgh are losers here because you don’t usually have to get tickets for this. What’s more, you don’t usually have to pay to access the event. It’s just as free as the rest of the Tour. In fact, this is the first time since 2014 – the last time the UK held the race – that tickets have been required.

I understand the need to organise crowds and generate revenue, but it feels a shame to have paid-for tickets at an event with free access at its essence. If tickets were required for safety/logistics reasons, then they should have been free, just like at screenings for BBC shows or National Lottery events.

That said, there’s still a chance that you’ll be able to see the riders for free as they roll around Edinburgh that same evening. Insider tip: they have to park up somewhere nearby for the obligatory rider photoshoot and press conferences before the presentation begins.

The post Winners and losers of the 2027 Tour de France route appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: In the Drops: Panaracer’s durable race tyres, Silca’s drip wax update, Coospo’s rear radar, Icesupp performance lollies, and the Canadian Rizzler
entry.content:
Cyclist
In the Drops: Panaracer’s durable race tyres, Silca’s drip wax update, Coospo’s rear radar, Icesupp performance lollies, and the Canadian Rizzler

It’s Friday, it’s In the Drops, the clocks go back (I think?) this weekend, we’re officially locked in for winter. But seriously can someone tell me if we’re gaining or losing sleep and can we stop this nonsense and just keep one time throughout the year? We’re all adults here we can deal with that surely?

The big story in the cycling world this week is the full routes for the 2027 Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes have been unveiled, you can find our stage-by-stage breakdown of the men’s route here and the women’s route here.

That’s far from the only thing we’ve had on the website, though. There was big computer news, with Coros’s very interesting super-thin Dura 2, which will practically never run out of battery unless you live in the far northern hemisphere in winter, as well as Garmin’s new 1060 plus Explore updates.

We’ve also published reviews of the also very interesting Ekoï PW8 pedals and tidy Asgard Access Plus shed, and there are more excellent articles coming today to spend your weekend reading.

Right, enough of that, we’re freewheeling into the weekend it’s time to get In the Drops.

Panaracer Agxero tyres

‘Race-day speed with the puncture protection to keep you rolling’ is how Panaracer describes the Agxero tyres. Sold.

More specifically, the Agxeros have been designed to combine the speed of very good Agilest tyres with added durability thanks to the use of a new ZSG Agile-X compound, which brings lower rolling resistance as well as improved grip and puncture resistance.

They come in 28c and 30c, weighing a claimed 270g and 300g respectively, and there are options for black or tan sidewalls. This particular set are the 30mm tanwalls, which couldn’t come at a better time for me as my bike currently has a 28mm tyre on the front and a 32mm on the back because the 28mm rear sidewall got slashed and 32mm is a bit tight of a squeeze for non-dry summer riding.

  • Buy now from Panaracer (£64.99)

Silca Super Secret 2.0 chain lube

Drip wax changed my life in 2026, I had a tester bottle, tried it, and have ridden with a massive smile and a healthier drivetrain ever since.

The second generation of Silca’s Super Secret drip wax was made in collaboration with Visma-Lease a Bike and the brand says the new formula both lasts longer than the first and has vastly improved wet-weather performance.

Silca claims that while hot wax is still cleaner and lasts longer, Super Secret 2.0 has near-identical efficiency and protection. That’s enough for a lazy so-and-so like me who tends to value ease of use very highly.

  • Buy now from Silca (£25)

Coospo TR70 Smart Radar tail light

Coospo’s TR70 rear radar and light has a 220° light with seven modes for all conditions to be seen on the road whenever you ride.

It can connect to both bike computers and phones to keep the rider aware of the traffic up to 140m away, even providing an alert when a vehicle comes around a blind bend, and it also has an emergency brake alert.

The TR70 is IP67 dust and waterproof, weighs a claimed 64g, and the mount and adapter make it compatible with different seat post shapes. Coospo claims battery lasts for up to 50 hours.

  • Buy now from Coospo (£77.72)

Icesupp lollies

Icesupp does what it says on the tin: it’s an ice lolly and a nutritional supplement in one package – perfect for training in hot temperatures but also if you’re having trouble getting food down.

They’re made with real fruit, include 5g protein and 2.5g fibre per 100g as well as key vitamins, and can be eaten either as a lolly or defrosted slightly to drink as a smoothie, with two potential ways to open the pouch for each use.

  • Buy now from Icesupp (£27.75, 12-pack)

What we’re into this week: Quebecois culture

If you’ve not seen this you are in for the treat of the century. In the last month, the internet has been swept by videos from French Canadian TV show Soirée Canadienne, which ran from 1960 to 1983 in Quebec. In particular clips of call-and-response folk songs, with the two most popular, absolute earworms fronted by a pair of charismatic kids, Serge Veilleux and Joël Legendre.

Veilleux’s is the most popular one online, partially because it looks as if the footage has been enhanced by AI to make it clearer, which adds a very weird visual aspect to the song about a dodgy doctor who keeps chopping off body parts. Veilleux, who has been dubbed the Canadian Rizzler, is a fantastic performer and demolishes this performance. I challenge you not to get stuck singing this all day.

The other one, which is the French folk song ‘J’ai vu le loup‘ (I saw the wolf), I actually prefer; it’s musically more interesting and gives me Les Choristes vibes.

Consider this the perfect way to round out Quebec’s big cycling year.

Ad feature

BOYD Cycling Expands Junior Wheel Trade-In Programme to UK

BOYD Cycling is bringing its annual Trade-In for Juniors programme to the UK this October, partnering with Kent-based Cyclopark Charity to help more young riders access quality equipment.

Throughout October, cyclists can trade in any wheelset, regardless of brand, model or condition, and receive 20% off a new BOYD wheelset.

Traded-in wheels will be inspected, refurbished where possible, and donated to young cyclists facing barriers to participation.

The initiative gives old wheels a second life while helping inspire the next generation of riders.

Trade in online at boydcycling.com or through participating BOYD Cycling retailers.

Find out more

Ad feature ends

entry.title: Priority Bicycles’ E-Sauce Is a Versatile, Low-Maintenance, Single Speed… E-Klunker?
entry.content:
As ebikes infiltrate the cycling world, we’re seeing motors and batteries added to all styles of bicycle, and it does beg the question: would it really hurt to offer pedal assist on any type of bike? Inspired by the success of their non-assisted Sauce single-speed MTB, Priority Bicycles went ahead and added a motor to create the new E-Sauce.

Yes, it’s a single-speed e-bike, designed for urban and light trail riding. It’s driven by a Gates belt drive system, and with the ability to host front and rear racks, it can haul plenty of cargo. As the nearest thing I’ve yet seen to an e-klunker, it does offer a lot of versatility despite its simplicity.

“We have had great success with our e-Coast beach cruiser line and wanted to bring something more versatile to our electric lineup,” said Connor Swegle, co-founder of Priority Bicycles. “The E-Sauce is that perfect mix of performance and ruggedness for any surface, with simplicity and low-maintenance aspects that make a Priority bicycle easy to take on a quick spin around the city.”

Priority E-Sauce – Key Specs and Features:

The E-Sauce features a 6061 aluminum hardtail frame, with a 100mm SR Suntour XCM 32 front suspension fork. The bike rolls along on 27.5” wheels featuring double-walled alloy rims and 2.4” WTB Intersector multisurface tires.

Priority equips all their bikes with Gates carbon belt drive, a low-maintenance system with a long-lasting drive belt that requires no lubrication. The single-speed E-Sauce comes with a 55t front sprocket and a 20t rear cog. All-weather stopping power is ensured by 2-piston hydraulic disc brakes on 180mm rotors.

Keeping things fun and your riding position comfortable is an 80mm rise, 740mm wide BMX-style handlebar, bolted to a 50mm stem. One nice touch included on the E-Sauce is a sealed bearing headset.

A Selle Royal Essenza saddle offers comfort without bulk, and Priority includes a set of composite pedals with chromoly spindles. The E-Sauce also comes with a frame-mounted rear kickstand.

For nighttime riding, the bike includes a front headlight mounted to the handlebar and a rear light built into the seatpost.

The E-Sauce is the first Priority bike to include their new Headway cargo mount. The mount allows you to bolt a front cargo rack directly to the bike’s head tube. If you don’t have a rack attached, a Priority head tube badge covers the mount neatly. This frame-mounted design keeps the weight of the cargo from affecting your steering. Priority’s Headway Front Cargo Rack (sold separately) can carry up to 55 lbs.

Out back, the E-Sauce frame offers mounts for standard pannier racks as well, providing more options for hauling cargo or attaching child seats. There is one water bottle mount on top of the bike’s down tube.

The E-Sauce weighs 59 lbs complete. Its max capacity is 300 lbs (rider, bike, and cargo). Frames are available in two sizes – S/M or M/L. These sizes should accommodate riders from 5’4” to 6’2”.

Drive System:

Powering the E-Sauce is a 750W rear hub motor, with five assist levels and a throttle mode. This is the most powerful motor Priority stocks on any of their bikes. It uses both torque and cadence sensors to ensure smooth, natural-feeling power delivery.

The E-Sauce ships out in a Class 2 configuration, assisting up to 20mph, but it can be adjusted to assist up to Class 3/28mph with pedal assist only – The throttle stops assisting at 20 mph to keep the bike from exceeding many state and local regulations. Priority recommends checking your local laws to ensure compliance.

Providing the juice for the E-Sauce is a 720Wh battery integrated into the down tube. The bike’s range is listed at anywhere from 20-60 miles depending on terrain, assist level, rider weight, etc. The battery is easily removable from the frame and can be charged in or off the bike. A key locks the battery into the bike, and the push of a button releases it when unlocked. A full battery charge takes about 4 hours.

A display unit sits on the left side of the handlebar. Its backlit display shows your assist level, speedometer, tripometer, and odometer, powers the bike on/off, plus controls the lights and activates walk mode. The twist-grip throttle is integrated into the right grip.

MSRP for the E-Sauce is $2199. It comes in the colorway shown above and is available now through Priority’s website.

prioritybicycles.com

entry.title: BH Ultralight <700g Road Bike is More Aero, Of Course Lighter & More Affordable
entry.content:
BH updated their Ultralight road bike, once again making it more aerodynamic, even as they shave grams away. Now 11% lighter than its predecessor, at less than 700g for the frame. Plus, it also gets a 12% aero drag reduction, care of subtly refined Kamm tails & other tube shaping. The fact that it’s also quite a bit cheaper – from the entry 105 level to the top-tier, UCI-illegal weight Dura-Ace level – is simply icing on the cake.

No more need to pick a lightweight climber’s bike or an aerodynamic sprinter’s bike. Just get one Ultralight.

2027 BH Ultralight and aerodynamic carbon road bike

The new MY27 BH Ultralight looks pretty similar to the version they launched back in 2023 to upgrade the aerodynamic performance of their lightweight road bike. But this new one is both lighter and more aero, developed in CFD together with the University of the Basque Country (EHU). And it’s still as stiff as before, creating a solid all-rounder for fast riding whether heading to the mountains, sticking to the flats, or all the rolling terrain in between.

What else is new?

Dropping the frame under 700g makes the new BH Ultralight one of the lightest production bikes on the market these days. But there are other updates besides its improved aerodynamics, too.

For one, BH finally gives the Ultralight bigger tire clearance. Officially, it’s only 32mm, because of the number of ultrawide rims out there. But they say that most 35mm tires will fit, with their required 6mm clearance between the frame & fork at its closest point.

They’ve also refined the bike’s geometry around a steep 74° seat tube angle for more forward weight balance. And BH claim new super short 405mm chainstays for faster acceleration and a more “direct responsive ride feel”. Although their geometry tables still show the same 410mm stays of the previous generation.

“The result is a bike that moves beyond the traditional concept of a pure climbing machine to embrace a much more versatile approach. The new Ultralight retains weight figures that place it among the lightest road bikes in its category, but now combines this advantage with more efficient aerodynamics, greater integration and clearance for wider tyres. It is designed to accelerate quickly on climbs, but also to maintain high speeds, tackle technical descents and compete effectively on a wide variety of routes.”

Tech details

  • hi-mod Toray T1100G carbon monocoque frame
  • ‘Air Bow’ aerodynamic tapered steer, full carbon fork
  • Hollow Core Internal Molding (HCIM) for ECL Evo carbon layup
  • claimed tire clearance up to 35mm (guaranteed max 32c tire clearance on wide rims)
  • fully integrated internal cable routing through the headset
  • electronic shifting only
  • proprietary D-shaped aero seatpost with hidden wedge-style clamp
  • integrated Planck taillight magnetically attaches to the post (included on top models)
  • new lightweight, 55mm deep BH Evo Stealth aero carbon wheels (included on top models)
  • PressFit BB386 EVO bottom bracket
  • flat mount disc brakes
  • lightweight machined 12mm thru-axles with integrated hidden levers
  • UDH rear, removable front derailleur braze-on mount
  • UCI-approved frame
  • 5 frame sizes (XS-XL)

2027 BH Ultralight – Pricing, options & availability

The new Ultralight is available on five stock frame sizes (XS-XL), three standard frameset colors (marbled red, crystalline white & raw black carbon), and the BH Unique custom paint program. Four complete builds of the new bike are on offer, all with Shimano Di2 electronic groupsets and all with a new unnamed one-piece carbon integrated Vision cockpit.

The 2027 BH Ultralight 6.0 sells for 5000€ (12% less than the previous generation) with 105 Di2 and Vision TC45 carbon wheels. At 7000€, the Ultralight 7.0 upgrades to Ultegra Di2 and SC45 wheels. Then, at 7500€, the Ultralight 8.0 adds a powermeter crankset to the Ultegra groupset, and includes the Planck taillight. Plus, the 8.0 adds BH’s own new 1350g Evo Stealth 55mm deep, 23mm internal carbon wheels with aero-bladed carbon spokes and ceramic bearings.

At the top-tier, the 8500€ BH Ultralight 9.0 gets a Dura-Ace group, the BH Evo Stealth wheels, and the Planck taillight. That’s a 15% lower price than the same spec level four years ago, and now in a bike that claims a complete weight of just 6.7kg (size S, without pedals).

The new bikes will be available in BH dealer bike shops starting in November, while custom-painted BH Unique bikes would start shipping at the end of January.

BHbikes.com

entry.title: Tour de France Femmes 2027 full route revealed with Puy de Dôme set to host explosive finale
entry.content:
Cyclist
Tour de France Femmes 2027 full route revealed with Puy de Dôme set to host explosive finale

The Tour de France Femmes 2027 route has been unveiled today alongside the men’s route, with nine stages starting in Leeds on Friday 30th July and coming to a dramatic finale on the legendary Puy de Dôme on Saturday 7th August.

Three stages in England get things underway including a central London team time-trial – a first for the Tour de France Femmes, before heading across the Channel, where a couple of punchy stages and a sprint await before the climbs come calling.

Two of the three stages in the mountains are summit finishes, including the enormous finale on the steep slopes of the Puy de Dôme, which finishes off a stage that packs in nearly 4,000m of elevation.

Tour de France Femmes 2027 key information 

  • Dates: Friday 30th July – Saturday 7th August
  • Grand Départ: Leeds, England
  • Finale: Puy de Dôme, France
  • Total kilometres: 1,156km
  • Total elevation gain: 17,665m
  • Total prize money: €250,000
  • Live television coverage: TNT Sports, HBO Max, TG4, SBS, Sky Sport, NBC/Peacock, FloBikes, France Télévisions, ARD
  • 2026 winner: Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez)
  • Most overall wins: 2 – Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez)

Tour de France Femmes 2027 route 

The 2026 Tour de France Femmes starts in Leeds, which welcomed the men’s peloton for the 2014 Grand Départ. But while that day culminated in a sprint at Harrogate, this race will see the women battle it out in Manchester to decide the first yellow jersey of the race. With Manchester to Sheffield on Stage 2 comes the hills, including several British classics, and that should see the maillot jaune change hands straight away.

Stage 3 hosts the first team time-trial in the Tour de France Femmes’s short history. There will be no individual TT in 2027, so the specialists will have to rally their teams to make the most of the 18km route and those GC contenders who are weaker against the clock will be hoping their teammates can keep them in the fight.

After that it’s over to France for Stage 4 for what should be a sprint, but there are enough hills for an attack to get away. Stage 5 is a true hilly day out, with six climbs at the tail-end of the route plus an uphill finish. There’ll be chance for a breather the following day, which is flat as a pancake.

The mountains come calling on Stage 7, which features the first of two proper summit finishes on La Loge des Gardes, where climbing legs should still be relatively fresh. Stage 8 sees the road to Clermont-Ferrand packed with ascents with six categorised climbs before a downhill run into town for the finish.

Stage 9 is the jewel in the crown of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes. It’s the longest day of the race, with elevation topping over 3,800m, with climbing straight out the gate. Seven categorised climbs will soften the legs before the explosive last dance on the legendary slopes of the Puy de Dôme volcano.

Tour de France Femmes 2027 stage-by-stage preview

Stage 1: Friday 30th July, Leeds – Manchester, 86km

The Tour de France Femmes begins in Leeds in 2027. Home to cycling greats including Millie Robinson, who lived there in 1955 when she won the first ever women’s Tour de France, Leeds hosted the men’s Tour for the start of the race in 2014, and will host the Tour de France Femmes’s UK debut next year.

After rolling out into Yorkshire a trio of Francified climbs will keep riders on their toes as they leave the county to finish the first stage in Manchester, where it will almost certainly be a bunch sprint.

Stage 2: Saturday 31st July, Manchester – Sheffield, 154km

The race stays in Manchester overnight to get an early night before a hectic Stage 2 to Sheffield via a selection of classic British hills. Staples of the hill climb scene in Winnats Pass and Snake Pass – which not even the Tour de France dares to rename – will split the bunch, and a trio of climbs will make the selection for the finale in Sheffield. Even Lorena Wiebes will struggle to hold onto yellow on a day like this.

Stage 3: Sunday 1st August, London – London, 18km (TTT)

On Stage 3, the Tour de France Femmes’s first ever team time-trial hits central London, where they should be met by big crowds on the 18km route, which takes in pretty much every landmark possible on the way to the finish on the Mall.

Stage 4: Monday 2nd August, Le Touquet-Paris-Plage – Calais, 123km

Stage 4 begins in the same location on the north coast of France as Stage 4 in the 2014 men’s Tour, when Marcel Kittel won the sprint finish.

Riders will navigate a series of short but punchy hills towards Calais, with the final climb the Côte du Cap Blanc-Nez, which featured in the 2022 men’s Tour, where Wout van Aert took a solo win in the yellow jersey. With that in mind, this could well see a split bunch reach Calais, but teams will be well aware of what could happen, so don’t rule out a sprint.

Stage 5: Tuesday 3rd August, Neufchâtel-en-Bray – Magnanville, 161km

Eight categorised climbs are packed into the Classics-like Stage 5, which will almost certainly see a very select group reach Magnanville for a punchy uphill finish. They’re far from the hardest climbs in the race, but all just about tick over a kilometre in length and hide stinging gradients, including a couple average north of 10%.

Stage 6: Wednesday 4th August, Orléans – Bourges, 138km

At long last, Stage 6 provides a certified sprint stage, and it will be the last one as the mountains are coming. Given the lack of flat days, this could be decisive for the green jersey competition.

Stage 7: Thursday 5th August, Nevers – La Loge des Gardes, 155km

Stage 7 will be a tense affair, with 100km of pan flat riding before the climbing starts. The road starts to head upwards long before the race officially hits a categorised climbs, with plenty of uncategorised climbing before the 2.1km of the Côte du Point du Jour brings the first mountain points of the day.

A brief downhill follows before the peloton hits La Loge des Gardes.

At nearly 7km in length, it’ll be enough for a proper GC battle, with the gradient sticking around 8% for almost the entire climb. This test should see the hierarchy start to form, but there are two tough stages incoming to defend positions.

Stage 8: Friday 6th August, La Bourboule – Clermont-Ferrand, 151km

Stage 8 has climbing from the start in La Bourboule, with six categorised test to battle it out on. After the final ascent on the Côte de Charade, the peloton speeds descends into Clermont-Ferrand for a fast finish, likely either for one solo leader or a sprint for just two or three.

Stage 9: Saturday 7th August, Clermont-Ferrand – Puy de Dôme, 170km

The final stage is the Queen Stage in its truest form, with the most kilometres and the most elevation – it’s also this year’s Etape du Tour de France Femmes. Unlike 2026’s Mont Ventoux stage, which was flat before the Bald Mountain, there are a mass of smaller climbs to contend with before the decisive finish on the mythical Puy de Dôme.

Whoever wins on the Puy de Dôme will write their name into cycling folklore, with its list of conquerors packed with big names including in the Tour de France Féminin, with Maria Canina taking the stage in both 1986 and 1988. It was last scaled in the men’s race in 2023 when Michael Woods broke Matteo Jorgenson’s heart with no fans watching roadside.

It has a deceptive start, easing off from its 7.5% gradient after just 3km, but the final 4km are consistently over 11% for a brutal sting in the tail.

Will Demi Vollering make it three yellow jersey wins or will someone else be crowned atop the volcano?

The post Tour de France Femmes 2027 full route revealed with Puy de Dôme set to host explosive finale appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Juliana Bicycles Announces the End of Its 13-Year Run as Santa Cruz’s Sister Brand
entry.content:
Last week, Juliana Bicycles quietly ceased independent operations with an announcement on its website saying, “Forward Together: Juliana and Santa Cruz as one brand.” Of course, the two brands have been very closely linked all along, but this announcement marks the end of an era for the pioneering women’s mountain bike brand. Since 2013, Juliana has operated as a standalone sister brand to Santa Cruz with separate operations, branding, and its own identity, helping inspire more women to get out and ride.

The Juliana story started years before it became a brand. In 1999, Santa Cruz debuted the first women’s-specific mountain bike named the “Juliana,” after mountain bike legend Juli Furtado. Fourteen years later, Juliana Bicycles spun off from Santa Cruz, becoming a standalone brand producing numerous women’s-specific models and operating more or less independently. 

While Juliana’s frames have always been essentially identical to their Santa Cruz counterparts, they typically featured lighter shock tunes and different touchpoints to suit female riders. Of course, the bikes also stood out with different paint jobs, branding, sponsorships, and marketing intended to inspire women to ride and feel welcome in a male-dominated sport. 

The Next Chapter

On the Juliana website, they call this the next chapter, and say, “It’s always been more about the rider on the bike than the name on the downtube. Juliana’s goal was to create a space for women to be seen, heard, and recognized. We don’t think it’s absolutely mission accomplished, but we believe that now is the time to bring our sister brand into the same tent and solidify that space for the future.”

While Juliana-branded bikes will no longer be produced, Santa Cruz will continue to maintain the Juliana website. There, Juliana owners can still make warranty claims or reference the archives for model information. On that note, Juliana warranties will still be honored, but handled by Santa Cruz. If you’re a Juliana owner, julianabicycles.com still has everything you need.

A Couple Takeaways

The industry has almost completely shifted away from women’s specific bikes. A decade ago, many of the major mountain bike brands, including Specialized, Cannondale, and Canyon, had women’s-specific models in their lineups. Over the years, those brands slowly phased them out in favor of unisex models and their bottom lines, leaving Juliana and Liv as the last women’s brands standing. Not because women don’t have different bike fit needs than men, but perhaps because those fit needs can now be met with today’s unisex models and sizing. There’s certainly no shortage of bikes and sizes to choose from these days.

Additionally, the discontinuation of the Juliana brand is undoubtedly linked to the ongoing belt-tightening across the industry. Santa Cruz and Juliana, among other brands, are owned by Pon.Bike. Yes, the same Pon.Bike that announced the closure of Cannondale’s Connecticut offices just yesterday. Beyond eliminating some redundancy, consolidating Juliana’s operations under the Santa Cruz name is surely another cost-saving measure, as is moving Cannondale’s North American operations to the West Coast to join them next year.  

More info at: julianabicycles.com

entry.title: WTB Launches 1,300-gram CMR Light Carbon XC Wheels
entry.content:
Today, WTB is adding to its lineup of carbon mountain bike wheels with the launch of the CMR Light wheelset. This new XC-oriented wheelset pairs lightweight high-performance carbon rims with WTB’s World Cup-proven Frequency 7X hubs to deliver wheels “built for speed, but engineered to last.” WTB says they were designed for riders seeking to maximize climbing efficiency while maintaining a lively and responsive ride feel both on the race course and off. 

CMR Light Wheels Details

Just about three weeks ago, WTB introduced its new CGR i28 Carbon Gravel wheels. Now, the new CMR Light slots into the brand’s lineup for the XC crowd with a different rim shape/profile but utilizing the same Frequency 7X hubs. Here’s what you need to know.

Frequency 7X Hubs

WTB is clearly proud of its new Frequency 7X hubs and highlights them before any other part of the new CMR Light wheels. These are the same hubs raced by the Cannondale Factory Racing team on the World Cup XC circuit this year. That includes Luca Martin, who rode them to multiple World Cup victories, podiums, and the overall XCC and XCO titles. When WTB says World Cup-proven, that’s what they mean.

One of WTB’s main talking points for the 7X hubs is the DLC (Diamond-Like Coating) on its ratchets. This reportedly increases the ratchet’s hardness while also significantly reducing friction compared to hard-plated chrome. Additionally, the inner ratchet ring uses a patent-pending splined interface, instead of threads, which is claimed to withstand twice the torque of threaded designs and makes it easier to service. It isn’t specified in our press materials, but we count 36 teeth on those DLC ratchets, which results in 10 degrees between engagement points.

On top of that, WTB says it uses “larger-than-typical” Enduro bearings throughout, including the freehub, which it claims increases the load rating per bearing by up to 38%. The stated benefits of this are a stiffer axle assembly, greater reliability, and longer service intervals. 

The Frequency 7X hubs are designed for use with straight-pull spokes and centerlock brake rotors. They come in regular Boost 15x110mm / 12x148mm axle spacing only, with options for SRAM XDR and Shimano Micro Spline freehub bodies.

Lightweight Carbon Rims

Light is in the name of the new CMR Light wheelset, and WTB designed a purpose-built lightweight carbon rim for the application. According to WTB, it has been engineered to deliver strength, stiffness, and impact resistance while also balancing small-bump compliance and precise, responsive handling. 

Like most modern mountain bike rims, the CMR Light has a 30mm internal width optimized for today’s tire width and profiles. It has a hookless bead and a wide bead top to help reduce the chances of pinch flats. Each rim has 24 spoke holes with external reinforcement and 4D spoke drillings to optimize load distribution. Of course, the rims also include WTB’s patented TCS technology for reliable tubeless performance.

Lightweight Design

According to WTB, the complete CMR Light i30 wheelset weighs in at 1,300 grams (front: 609g, rear: 691g), including valves and rim tape. While there are obviously lighter XC wheelsets on the market, that’s still pretty light and competitive with similar high-performance models like DT Swiss’s XRC 1200 Spline (1,303 grams), for example.

Specs

  • Rim: Carbon
  • Size: 29” only
  • Internal rim width: 30mm
  • Spoke count: 24, straight-pull
  • Hub: Frequency 7X w/ DLC ratchets
  • Rotor Interface: Centerlock
  • Freehub bodies: SRAM XD, Shimano Micro Spline
  • Weight: 1,300 grams (front: 609g, rear: 691g)

Ride With Confidence

Like its other carbon rims, WTB backs the new CMR Light with its Ride With Confidence Guarantee. “If you break a WTB carbon rim while riding, as long as you’re the original owner, we’ll send you a replacement for free. No exceptions.”

Pricing

  • USD: Front $850 /Rear $950 / Wheelset $1,800
  • EUR: Front €727.45 /Rear €822.45 / Wheelset €1,549.90
  • GBP: Front £609.50 /Rear £689.50 / Wheelset £1,299

Availability

The new CMR Light wheels are available directly from the brand or through authorized North American and European WTB dealers. Head to the WTB website to learn more or find a dealer near you.

wtb.com

entry.title: Smart cycling tech just got a whole lot smarter
entry.content:
Cyclist
Smart cycling tech just got a whole lot smarter

Since its inception in December 2015, Chinese-based cycling brand Magene has blazed a trail in forward-thinking smart devices and cycling technology, making our rides more convenient and helping us push the boundaries of performance.

The level of trust placed in the company’s products has even led to its sponsorship of numerous UCI Continental squads as well being a team partner of UCI WorldTeam XDS Astana since early 2026, supplying technical support and products to a team racing at the highest level. And now, with a comprehensive overhaul of its global identity, the brand is not only refreshing its appearance but also continuing to push the boundaries of technological development.

The story so far

This rebrand builds on more than a decade of growth and innovation. Founded in 2015, Magene has been dedicated to smart cycling technology, with a comprehensive portfolio spanning smart GPS computers, smart trainers, power meters, sensors and smart lights. Together, these products provide connected solutions for a wide range of indoor and outdoor riding needs. As Magene continues to grow, the brand is expanding its presence in international markets and further strengthening its position as a professional smart cycling brand you really need to know about.

But the rebrand goes beyond simply a refreshed visual identity. Magene is focused on continuing to advance its brand philosophy, product technology, and customer experience, marking the beginning of a new chapter in its development.

The vision

Through a unified brand identity, Magene aims to strengthen its connection with cycling around the world. And, as discerning cyclists familiar with the early days of a certain grey-and-pink UK kit brand, or visitors to certain bright orange-branded virtual cycling worlds, know, this starts with colour.

Magene’s refreshed colour system retains what the brand calls ‘Energy Orange’ as its brand signature (which embodies the spirit of competition), alongside ‘Performance Blue’ to signify professionalism and precision. The core palette is completed with low-saturation, neutral tones which they’ve dubbed ‘Elite Grey’ and ‘Metallic Silver’. In terms of visual style, it’s a purposefully restrained choice of tones which – alongside a simplified design – the brand says ‘returns to an authentic experience and strengthens users’ perception of professional performance’.

The thinking behind the brand’s new logo also comes from a considered approach. Now featuring the company’s name in capital letters, the italicisation of the custom typeface is designed to convey a sense of speed, dynamic energy, and movement.

Forging onwards

The future is bright for Magene. Beyond the fact that its rebrand will no doubt strengthen brand recognition, understanding, and consumer trust across the world, the job of continuing to develop and refine its products continues at full pace. At its heart, Magene aims to deliver better solutions for cyclists, with intelligent products designed for all scenarios. And this will only be enhanced with its pro cycling connections.

The brand’s newly formed bond with UCI WorldTeam XDS Astana involves the supply of smart GPS bike computers, smart trainers, smart radar tail lights and heart rate sensors. By getting these products on the bikes of riders competing at the top of their game, Magene will receive invaluable feedback from pro racers – as well as race data and product testing insights – that will directly influence product development.

Backing up the rebranding of Magene with products that are proven on the world stage, as well as with internal R&D innovation, will not only improve the overall user experience but also strengthen the position of this exciting brand across the globe.

To learn more about Magene’s products, visit www.magene.com

entry.title: BlackHeart Bike Co Road Ti
entry.content:
Today, BlackHeart Bike Co. introduces the new evolution of Road Ti. A reflection of modern carbon aesthetics in a metal form, built to last. The latest version brings over the 3D-printed details that make a difference, first introduced on the Road Plus Ti earlier this year, making BlackHeart’s Road Ti a fast, refined road bike…

Road Ti Details

The ride stays true to the original. Premium 3/2.5 double-butted titanium tubing and dropped, slightly curved seatstays deliver a smooth yet snappy ride, while a kammtail downtube, one-piece carbon cockpit, and fully integrated cabling give little away to the fastest bikes on the road, regardless of material. Pro fit geometry keeps the handling quick and sharp. It carries forward the ride characteristics that earned the previous Road Ti Cyclingworld Europe’s 2024 Best Race Bike award, now paired with a more refined, modern platform.

The same thoughtful 3D-printed frame elements found on the Road Plus Ti, named one of Bicycling Magazine’s 2026 Best Bikes, now come to the Road Ti. A seamless seat tube cutout adds tire clearance and room for fenders. The T47-68 bottom bracket shell features a lower channel with a retaining clip for cleaner brake hose routing, while a solid brake mount with a self-guiding hose port makes building and servicing the bike simpler.

Finishing

Each frame is reamed, chased, and faced at the factory, ensuring it is build-ready straight out of the box. Consistent with the entire BlackHeart line, the Road Ti is backed by a lifetime warranty against manufacturing defects for the original owner.

In collaboration with ENVE, SRAM and Zipp, signature launch editions are now also available.

BlackHeart Road Ti Geo

BlackHeart also offers its Perfect Fit Program to help riders get it right the first time. Riders can book a free 30-minute 1:1 consultation with the team to dial in size, build spec, and geometry, using their own measurements and current bike as a reference point. It’s part of a human-first approach to customer service, backed by a fit guarantee: if a rider who completed the Perfect Fit Program is unhappy with their size, BlackHeart covers shipping to swap it for a different frame size.

Road Ti Specs

  • BlackHeart Road Ti Frameset – $3,499
    • Includes frame, ENVE fork, seatpost, headset
    • +$300 for custom fork paint – we can match any automotive paint available BlackHeart Road Ti Signature Builds – starting from $5,799
    • Includes BlackHeart Carbon barstem, SRAM Rival AXS or Shimano 105 Di2 groupset, and Hunt Allroad Alloy wheels.
  • BlackHeart Road Ti ENVE Edition – $13,749
    • SRAM Red AXS 2X Power groupset, ENVE SES Aero Pro barstem V2, ENVE SES 4.5 Pro Carbon wheelset, ENVE Carbon seatpost,
    • CeramicSpeed Alpha BB
    • Size 56 = 17 lbs 0 oz
    • BlackHeart Road Ti Zipp Edition – $13,499
    • SRAM Red AXS 2X Power groupset, Zipp SL 80 Race Carbon Handlebar with Zipp SL Service Course Alloy stem, Zipp 202 NSW wheelset,
    • BlackHeart Carbon seatpost, CeramicSpeed Alpha BB
    • Size 56 = 16 lbs 12 oz
  • Available in 9 sizes to fit riders from 5’0″ to 6’7’
  • Tire clearance up to 700x35mm (with fenders)
  • 100% recyclable premium 3/2.5 double-butted titanium tubing
  • 3D-printed details carried over from the Road Plus Ti for real-world usability Removable direct mount front derailleur hanger
  • Cane Creek HCR headset, T47-68 bottom bracket, Round 31.6mm seatpost, UDH
  • 2x/1x electronic

The new Road Ti will be in stock in November at blackheartbikeco.com and through BlackHeart’s growing dealer network.

entry.title: BlackHeart Updates the Road Ti with 3D-Printed Details from the Road Plus Ti
entry.content:
Truckee, California’s BlackHeart Bike Co. just rolled out an updated Road Ti. This time, the titanium frame reflects a subtle carbon aesthetic with new 3D-printed highlights. But the 3/2.5 double-butted titanium, dropped and slightly curved seatstays, and pro-fit geometry mean that the titanium ride character stays. That formula helped the previous version grab Cyclingworld Europe’s 2024 Best Race Bike award. So yeah, leaving that part alone is a defensible call.

The Road Ti’s new 3D-printed details, which originally debuted on the Road Plus Ti earlier this year, trickle down to the new Road Ti. You get a seamless seat tube cutout for extra tire clearance and fender room. The main difference between the two? The Road Ti fits up to 35mm tires with fenders. The Road Plus Ti fits up to 42mm. There are other differences, but start there.

Also, a T47-68 bottom bracket shell with a lower channel and retaining clip for tidier brake hose routing, and a solid brake mount with a self-guiding hose port. Some of these features could lead to fewer colorful words in the garage when you’re building or servicing this beaut.

Race Bike Checklist

The rest reads like a modern race-bike checklist: kammtail downtube, one-piece carbon cockpit, and fully integrated cabling. BlackHeart says it gives little away to the fastest bikes on the road, regardless of material.

Frames are reamed, chased, and faced at the factory, so your mechanic doesn’t have to do it. The lifetime warranty against manufacturing defects covers the original owner.

BlackHeart Road Ti Geo

Signature launch editions with ENVE, SRAM, and Zipp are also available (see below). Then there’s the Perfect Fit Program: a free 30-minute 1:1 consult on size, spec, and geometry. If you complete it and still end up unhappy with your size, BlackHeart covers shipping for a swap. That’s kind of unheard of.
