entry.title: SSCXWC26BHAM: The Facilitators Made Me Do It – Summer Hanson, Bobby Arispe, Zach Hale, & Quinn Kelly
entry.content:
Summer Hanson raced the Women’s and Non-Binary (WNB) Single-Speed Cyclocross World Championships in Bellingham. Why? Because the facilitators made her do it…

“It won’t be where you left it,” a stranger tells me as I approach the bikes strewn in the mud at the start line. I lay my bike down, pausing to consider taking off my lights to hand them to someone I vaguely know nearby. “Don’t overthink it!” someone shouts at me. I leave the bike on the ground and run off to the crowd of women and non-binary folks on the other side of the imposing wooden gate.

Commanding facilitator voices direct us, “Walk backward! More! Okay, come back this way a little!” I’m jostling with ladies and theys with tops bursting to reveal pregnant bellies and titties with hamburger pasties. I’m swimming in colorful wigs, human banana slugs, and psychedelic quilted shark people. I am captivated by the most toned legs I’ve ever seen on display beneath stretchy daisy dukes.

Someone in a tutu compliments my outfit, admiring my confidence. I look down at my tiger-print underwear (with a tiger’s face on the butt) and tell them I’d planned to wear shorts, but after finding out we’d be watersliding into the quarry, I decided I’d rather not spend the rest of my day in wet denim. This is just what I had on underneath.

Better Together

A facilitator, Katie Staver, announces that this is the biggest field of women and nonbinary racers in a Single Speed Cyclocross World Championship race in its 20-year history, with around 100 women and 21 non-binary racers. I ponder the collective peer pressure that helped make this happen, and question how we are defining “world championship,” as I look around at the mostly white American (and perhaps some Canadian) people around me.

The Single Speed Cyclocross World Championship in Bellingham was only my second cyclocross race after stoking a tandem at last year’s Woodland Park Grand Prix. Until I removed the shifter and pushed in the derailleur limit screws on the ’90s Bianchi Advantage hybrid bike I borrowed from my workplace two days earlier, I had never ridden a singlespeed bike in my adult life. I’ve always thought singlespeeding seemed stupid and unnecessarily difficult, but I’m learning that’s the point. I’m here because of the storm of excitement in Seattle’s “alternative” cycling culture, not far from the glorious bike utopia of Bellingham, the event’s host city this year.

I’m a mechanic at Bike Works, a social justice-oriented bike nonprofit in South Seattle, whose work includes restoring and redistributing tons of used bikes that are donated by the community. It’s the type of job that people dream of doing when they retire, but it’s actually a job one can have, with some acceptance of being kind of cash poor, but rich in obscure vintage bike parts, tattered bike zines from the ’90s, and bike nerd friends to hang out with all day. I also organize events and lead social rides for Sound Break, a new bike shop and café in Pioneer Square that’s made its way onto the map as a community gathering place for local and traveling cyclists of all stripes.

Single Speed Fervor

My first introduction to the cumbersome acronym SSCXWC26BHAM was during the 7 Deadly Sins of Cyclocross, a cyclocross season kickoff ride/event that I helped promote at Sound Break alongside Becca Book and Rez (Justin Resnick), two facilitators of the World Championship event. The hype continued to drip into my ethosphere from my seasoned superiors at Bike Works. I’d been hearing breathless reviews of the Lookout Arts Quarry, this year’s race venue, from Recycle & Reuse Director Steve Gadingan. He described his otherworldly experience at the Sh’Bang Art Festival as we wrenched on bikes in the warehouse and urged me not to miss the rare chance to attend a bike event there. I’d never heard of SSCXWC before September, but the crazed look in Steve’s eyes convinced me to go watch the final race on Sunday.

A week or so after getting the low-down from Steve, my partner Quinn and I attended our second Lopez Island Time Trial (LITT), a kooky alleycat style campout + race, organized by SSCXWC facilitator Mike Udelhofen & co, in its second year open to the public (and longstanding tradition between friends before that). They offered 100 bonus points to those who registered to either volunteer or race at the SSCXWC26BHAM. As a defending trophy winner at the LITT, I was hungry for any points that were easier to earn than chugging a can of condensed tomato soup, so I signed up to volunteer.

I couldn’t make it to the qualifiers, and I didn’t ride single speed or cyclocross, so I didn’t exactly consider racing. The facilitators, many of whom were at the LITT, didn’t accept these excuses. Before my conversation with facilitator Becca Book ended that Saturday night at Spencer Spit State Park, I was handed a green SSCX26BHAM-branded zip tie for my derailleur and looped into an email thread with Katie, who assured me I could compete in just the Sunday championship race. Yes, Becca was facilitating whilst partying and camping; are you surprised?

I Tried Not To Race

I continued to attempt to weasel my way out of the race by trying to sign up for a volunteer shift, but all of the Sunday slots were closed. Turns out, sponsors adopted sections of the course, lightening the load for facilitators and volunteers. Evil, Transition, PNW Components, Kona, Outbound Lighting, and Cascade Cross all dialed in the course with obstacles, spectacles, smoke machines, jumps, etc. They wore full costumes and came stocked with handups (snacks or beverages that spectators hand to racers) and noisemakers to heckle us. With little race-day help needed, I offered my skills as a photographer and bike mechanic to the facilitators, and they met me with a resounding “RACE!!!” Finally, with a waived registration fee thanks to the Beard Scholarship Fund, and the facilitators’ appreciation for The Radavist, I finally surrendered to the inevitable. This, reader, is how to get over 100 women and nonbinary riders to sign up for a cyclocross race.

For my surrender, I was rewarded with the most fun race I have ever participated in: I slid down a waterslide into the quarry 3 times, biked through bubble and smoke machines, and rammed a 6′-tall beach ball with my front wheel, bouncing it high enough to bike underneath. I’m doused with buckets of water, whipped (with consent) by a dominatrix, and pushed up hills in a genuinely helpful manner. By my third lap, I worked up the courage to take a couple of jumps, screaming, “I’m so scared, I’m so scared!”

Along the way, I had four cherry tomatoes expertly popped into my mouth by strangers’ hands, as well as a pickle, an Oreo, three Nerds Gummy Clusters, several tiny cups and swigs of Rainier beer, bagged wine splashed on my face, a choked gulp of a mystery liquor from Steve’s gigantic flask, and a mouthful of a White Russian that I immediately spit all over the ground (thanks, but I’m vegan!). On multiple occasions, I peered into a cup as I drank the contents, only to see a healthy amount of dirt sprinkled in. That was just part of the experience!

During the race, communication was polite; plenty of “On your left!” At one point, I heard, “Mind if I take this descent first?” before witnessing a red fishnet-clad racer ahead of me skillfully bike down the gnarliest dirt descent on the course. Sheesh, I see you! My cyclocross skills might not have prepared me for the deranged obstacles of this course, but I rode 3 full laps, pushing my bike up hills and keeping my balance while riding 35 mm tires through some of the chonkiest gravel you ever did see. I put my heart into it, and I have the mysterious bruises to prove it.

Badminton

By afternoon, the sun was high in the sky for an unseasonably warm October day. I ran around photographing the men’s race, and swam to a floating dock in the quarry with the Wet Boyz. They’re Steve’s crew of Bellingham homies who brought the party to the waterslide area.

We rounded out the day with an afterparty at Structures Brewing on the waterfront in Bellingham, where delegations from Asheville and Missoula duked it out for next year’s hosting rights with a game of badminton, an obviously important part of singlespeed cyclocross dominance. The stamina of this haggard crowd to party on after three days of chaos sheds light on the depth of some of the long-distance friendships around me.

If the open arms that pulled me in were any indication, cyclists from around the world who like to push their limits without taking themselves too seriously will be warmly welcomed to Missoula next year.

The post SSCXWC26BHAM: The Facilitators Made Me Do It appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Industry Nine Revive 2.0 Wheelset Review – spencer harding
entry.content:
With Industry Nine‘s acquisition of We Are One, the Asheville, North Carolina-based company can keep the entire wheel manufacturing process in North America. The product of this merger, along with many other wheel combinations, is the WR1 Revive 2.0 gravel rims featuring I9 Solix classic hubs. The rims feature WR1’s Convergence technology and the Solix hub’s continuously phased engagement, yielding 605 points of engagement or .59 degrees. See what Spencer thought about these tech-filled wheels below…

Not to beat a dead horse too many times, but wheel reviews are difficult. Ron Lewis did a splendid job speaking to the difficulty with an eloquence I can’t match in his review of the Teravail  Fluent wheels recently. Wheels, by design, disappear and aren’t a contact point akin to saddles, grips, bars, or pedals. Wheels connect us to the ground, but even then they are buffered by the endless permutations of tire choices. I will do my darndest to dissect these wheels, but these are really high-end, machined in the US hubs and Canadian-made carbon rims, and to none’s surprise, they are sweet. I still remember the joy when I got to ride/review my first set of carbon wheels, which happened to be the same pairing of WR1 and I9, though this was prior to the acquisition. Many of my thoughts ring true from that review; carbon wheels are still frickin’ sweet, and the freehub noise is, likewise, a bit much.

Industry Nine Revive 2.0 Wheelset Quick Hits

  • Revive 2.0 Rims
    • Material: Carbon
    • Size: 700c
    • Hole Count: 24h & 28h
    • Internal Width: 25mm
    • Rim Depth: 19mm
    • ERD: 602.5mm
    • Weight: 360g (24h & 28h)
  • Hubs: SOLiX J-Bend
    • P.O.E: 605 points
    • Engagement: .59 degrees
    • Mechanism: Continuously phased, 5-pawl x 121-tooth drive ring
    • Spoke System: Direct-thread machined aluminum for System hub or J-Bend Steel (reviewed) on classic scalloped hubs.
    • Bearing Spec: Equalized spec, full-contact endcap seals + proximity dust/water shield
    • Preload System: Bore-diameter contraction – eliminates play, maximizes longevity
  • $1899 as reviewed
  • Freehub options: Campy N3w, HG-11, Microspline-R, and XDR.
  • Hub shell colors: Black, Bronze, Gold, Orange, Purple, Red, and Silver (reviewed)
  • Available in standard 12 x 100/142 thru axle and 9 x 100/135 QR
  • Spokes: I9 System alloy, Sapim CX-Ray bladed (reviewed), and Sapim Race

Revive 2.0 Rims With Convergence Technology

The most aesthetically pleasing part of the Revive 2.0 rims is the convergence pattern of the spoke bed. Each spoke is offset +/- 6 degrees from flat to perfectly align the spoke head and nipple for each spoke. The back-and-forth sinuous luge of the rim bed is as elegant as it is practical. Also, gotta shout out the name Convergence in the context of the company’s name, We Are One. Convergence really ties the room together; well played.

If you have worked on wheels at all, you have probably seen nipples pull through rims or cracking around the spoke holes. Convergence creates “360-degree full contact” between the nipple and rim. We have seen offset spoke beads to keep spoke length equal between both sides of the rim, but I haven’t seen a rim truly equalize the point pressure at the nipple/rim interface. I have experienced zero issues with the Revive Rims during my testing period, so I’ll have to believe their claim for now.

Solix Hubs

Featuring I9’s continuously phased freehub mechanism shared with their Hydra2 hubs, the Solix hubs have 605 points of engagement, creating a .59 degree of engagement. While that is not technically instant, it’s pretty damn close. Basically, you are never going to feel any lull in the engagement of these hubs when you put the hammer down. The five pawls each have three small teeth per pawl that allow the first pawl to engage nearly instantly, allowing the subsequent pawls to progressively engage to catch the coming torque. The 121-tooth drive ring and pawls are spaced as such that there is almost always a pawl engaging, unless you can feel .59 degree of slop in your pedal stroke, which you surely can not.

The Solix hubs feature low drag via reduced pawl spring pressure, smaller drive ring diameter, and relocated freehub seals. The axle and bearing layout has been updated with equalized bearing spec and the best seals I9 has used.

Setup

Now the only, and I mean the only, issue I had with these wheels was the tubeless tape, which may or may not have been the manufacturer’s issue. These wheels came to me after Miguel had too much on his plate, and when I set them up, I found something curious I had never come across before. The tubeless tape for this 25mm rim was something like 15mm and wrapped twice, but once on each side of the rim bed. This left a seam right on the spoke holes and subsequently led to slow leaks.

Miguel could not recall if he had the rim locally retaped or if it was factory spec. I9 mentioned that this style may have been used in the past before their acquisition of WR1, but that a new tape was being implemented at the moment. A simple wrap of some fresh tape and zero issues since then. Whatever the oversight or issue was, it was easily rectified. Do you tape rims like this? Im sure someone in the comments will tell me this is superior for saving 3 grams and 2.75 watts at 23 kph or some shit.

Wheels Disappear but the Buzz Lingers

With great design, we hope it just disappears from our perception. The convergence rim tech and incredible engineering of the I9 hubs mean I just forget about my wheels; they work flawlessly. The only reminder of all that tech, research, and machining is the damned freehub noise. I9 has toned down their freehub noise since the initial Hydra hubs, but the insane engagement of the Solix hubs comes with buzzing. Occasionally I’ll find myself becoming accustomed to the noise, but if I am on a downhill with friends, they tend to chide me about the noise.

I don’t know if I need absolutely silent Onyx hubs. My last foray into quieter pawls on WTB hubs led me down a rabbit hole of chasing every rattling zip tie or housing on my bike. The Solix hubs exist not as an absolute outlier in terms of buzz, but definitely far from the center. I think we have superseded the need to have loud hubs as a signifier of quality, or of just how impressive the engagement of your hubs is. I9, can we get quieter hubs just as exquisitely engineered as your loud hubs one day?

Warranty

When I encourage people to get carbon rims, it is usually after they have destroyed other rims, hubs, or just whole wheels. At that point, they need a warranty for their abusive riding. So, to that point, I find that above any engagement spec or weather seal, it is the warranty on the product I am curious about. I9 has a great warranty that includes:

  • Carbon Rims are covered for life against defects in material or workmanship, and impact damage while riding within the intended use of the wheel
    • They offer rim replacement or a factory rebuild for $100-125
  • Hubs are covered for five years against defects in material or workmanship.
    • For the first two years, coverage includes parts, labor, and return shipping. From years three through five, parts are covered, but labor and shipping are not. Bearings and other normal wear items are excluded

I didn’t get to test the warranty on this review, but the warranty is pretty damned comprehensive.

Conclusion

I have very much enjoyed my time on the Revive 2.0 rims. Minus the tape issue, the experience has been without fault. After many months of hard riding from rough pavement to low-class singletrack, the rims only show the slightest deviation from true, an amount I’d scarcely fix even if they happened to be rim brake wheels. My initial time with an incredibly high engagement I9 hub was on a mountain bike wheelset where the near-instantaneous engagement felt more necessary in techy rock sections. Being far from a performance gravel or road rider, that level of quick engagement felt unnecessary for my style of riding, but I’ll be damned if it wasn’t sweet. If you want to support domestic manufacturing, demand high engagement hubs, love anodized color options, and want impressively handcrafted carbon rims, the I9 Revive 2.0 wheelset might just be for you.

Pros

  • Lightweight carbon rims are fucking sweet
  • Near-instant engagement with Solix hubs
  • Lifetime warranty on rims
  • 5-year warranty on hubs
  • Convergence rim technology is as elegant as it is well engineered
  • Hubs (Asheville, NC) and Rims (Kamloops, BC) are North American-made

Cons

  • 25mm internal feels safe at the moment but behind the ever-wider tire trend in gravel
  • Only 24h and 28h rim options may leave folks accustomed to more spokes spooked; let the warranty soothe your concerns
  • Stock tape was an issue, but I9 has changed their tape in the interim
  • .59 degree engagement feels superfluous for gravel
  • Loud freehub noise can be distracting

See more at Industry Nine.

The post Industry Nine Revive 2.0 Wheelset Review appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Tailfin R&D Builds a Singular Peregrine Inspired by Pass Hunting
entry.content:
Inspired by Japanese Pass Hunting from the 1980s, UK bag company Tailfin pinged its in-house R&D company to develop a modern rendition of the classic Japanese sport to be displayed at the brand’s Bespoked Osaka booth this weekend. Let’s check it out!

Archival photos via @niigata0252

Pass Hunting

Pass hunting began in the 1980s as a non-competitive cycling and mountaineering sport focused on finding, riding, or carrying a bicycle over mountain passes. Both the Japanese and the French perfected and documented this adventurous form of cycling. Finding inspiration from over forty years of Pass Hunting, Tailfin pinged its R&D department to reimagine what a modern Tailfin lineup would look like if it were used in a traditional Pass Hunting setup.

In-House R&D

Tailfin’s prototyping department, whose workshop sits right next to the kitchen at Tailfin HQ, principally exists to build prototypes for the R&D Division, the brand’s roster of ultra athletes, kitting out some of the best ultra riders in the world with bleeding-edge bikepacking tech and enabling a fast, iterative way of developing products. A couple of times a year, the department also takes on an R&D Kitchen project, with one goal in mind: to have fun and experiment.

These projects have no commercial target. They are about creative freedom and play: throwing aside restrictive thinking and looking at things in a different way. Some ideas might come out of them, but that is not the goal. It’s fun, energizing, and very unserious. Tailfin’s usual briefs lean towards lighter and faster. On this one, the team asked themselves what they would want to take, and the answer was extra time and extra luxuries: a trip built around the stops rather than the distance.

Tailfin Inspiration

The kit started with a film camera, in keeping with an analog approach. Theo, from Tailfin’s product department, designed a front bag to carry it, with a map pocket for a real paper map, included for the romance of it. Molly reimagined one pannier as an insulated cool bag for cold beers and a refrigerated picnic, and made a separate bag for a small espresso maker. Callum, Soft Goods Prototyper, redesigned the frame bag with flip-top closures in place of zips. It is divided vertically rather than horizontally, with access at the front so it can be used while riding.

The rest of the kit includes a sketchbook, watercolors and pencils, a fishing rod, a Helinox chair and a towel, but no swimming costume, in case a remote wild swimming spot turns up.

Singular Peregrine Built For Pass Hunting

The result is a British take on that tradition, built around the new Singular Peregrine Mk5. Singular founder Sam Alison launched the Peregrine in 2008, combining fat tires, drop bars and disc brakes on a classically styled lugged steel frame, and it was a gravel bike before the category had a name. The fifth generation keeps that character and refines it.

The British-designed frame is paired with a mix of British and Japanese components, and with Tailfin’s own versions of two touring classics: low front panniers and a randonneur handlebar bag. Both are made in British waxed canvas that weathers naturally, and both use the same mounting hardware and stability engineering as Tailfin’s race gear.

Making the aesthetic British gave the team another muse: a friend of the team and Bristol tailor David Darby Minns, who brought fabric samples and books full of vintage tailoring, old waxed jackets and pictures of fly fishing.

The setup is not a product in development, though Tailfin expects ideas from the project to inform future work.

Where to See It

  • Bespoked Osaka, 23–25 October 2026, GLION Museum, Osaka, Japan. Press and trade day: Friday 23 October.
  • Kendal Mountain Festival, 19–22 November 2026, Kendal, UK.
  • Velofollies, 22–24 January 2027, Kortrijk Xpo, Belgium.

The post Tailfin R&D Builds a Singular Peregrine Inspired by Pass Hunting appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Campandgoslow Blue Lug Collection
entry.content:
Bar tape and accessory company Campandgoslow has been working with Tokyo bike shop Blue Lug as a supplier of its handlebar tape for years, but this marks the two brands’ first collaboration. Within this drop is a Tool Roll, Duckbill Cap, Triangle Reflector, and a Half Messenger Bag that can be used as a basket bag.

Camp + Blue Lug: Tool Roll $58.00

The Blue Lug Tool Roll is perfect for keeping your bag organized. With two drop-in pockets and a zipper compartment for your small stuff, it’ll fit your coffee kit, repair kit or a couple Kit Kat bars. You can also strap it underneath your saddle for bagless adventures, but all you off-roaders may want to swap in a Volié strap.

  • 1000D Cordura with Great Horned Owl, Brown Trout or Western Rattler trim
  • 500D Cordura with Eastern Rattler
  • Folded: 6.5″ tall x 5.25″ wide, Unfolded: 6.5″ tall x 15″ wide
  • Drop-in and zippered pockets: 5″ tall x 4.25″ wide
  • Adjustable locking buckle
  • Made by Blue Lug in Japan

Camp + Blue Lug: Duckbill Cap $46.00

The five-panel Duckbill Cap is made from water-repellent, breathable nylon and trimmed with our custom woven tape. The caps are designed with a relaxed silhouette so they are comfortable for wearing or stuffing in your pocket. On the back end, there is an adjustable webbing strap with a low-profile buckle.

  • One-size-fits-most with a max of 25″ head (8 hat size)
  • Unstructured, packable brim, length 2.75″

Camp + Blue Lug: Triangle Reflector $14.00

Everyone’s familiar with Blue Lug’s iconic Triangle Reflectors. We just added a few little touches with a trim tape loop and a center fabric that matches the tool rolls and messenger bags. These small but mighty reflectors fit pretty much anywhere on your bag or bike.

Do not leave different colors face to face for a long time as the color may transfer.

  • 3.3″
  • Made by Blue Lug in Japan

Camp + Blue Lug: Half Messenger Bag $125.00

This pared-down half-size messenger bag works well for commutes and grocery runs. It also easily drops into a Wald 137 basket when you’re ready to get the weight off your back.

  • 1000D Cordura with Great Horned Owl, Brown Trout or Western Rattler trim
  • 500D Cordura with Eastern Rattler
  • Nylon upper, tarpaulin lining
  • 2 inner pockets, 12.25″ wide x 9.5″ tall x 6″deep, longest point of flap 19.5″
  • Strap is 1.5″ with a metal adjuster buckle
  • Velcro closure with straps for carrying bulkier, oversized loads
  • Made by Blue Lug in Japan

entry.title: The Fauna XL Cargo Cage Is Here!
entry.content:
The XL Cargo Cage is an oversized version of Fauna’s original cage, which has been an aesthetic, functional, and affordable addition to the cargo cage market since launching last August. Building on that success, the XL keeps the same proven design as its smaller sibling, but doubles the carrying capacity from 3kg to 6kg. That means more room for stuff like the rain gear you don’t want to cautiously bring but probably should, or that extra cozy fleece for downtime at camp…

Fauna XL Cargo Cage Quick Hits

  • Body: 3 mm 304 stainless steel
  • Foot: 5 mm 304 stainless steel
  • Finish: Black sandtex powder coat, or raw tumbled stainless
  • Weight 185 g (body), 88 g (foot)
  • Includes 1× cage body, 1× foot, 3× M5 × 16 mm bolts, 3× TPU spacers
  • Made in Canada
  • Load Capacity Tested to 6 kg. Always consider the strength of your mounts, particularly on carbon frames.
  • Pricing
    • Single – $79.00 CAD/ $59.00 USD
    • Two Pack – $139.00 CAD/ $99.00 USD
  • Free Shipping Worldwide (over $25.00 CAD)

The XL also carries over the functionality of its petite predecessor, with an adjustable foot that raises and lowers to help dial in the perfect fit for whatever bag or cargo you’re carrying. The foot can be removed entirely to make room for extra-long cargo, shave off a few grams, or to pair the cage with Fauna’s Front Cargo System.

Fauna keeps it local, with production based in BC. The XL Cargo Cage is manufactured in Delta, and packaged right here in Vancouver. It’s built tough, pairing the 3mm tumbled 304 stainless steel body with a burly 5mm removable stainless steel foot. The body weighs in at 185g, with the foot adding another 88g for a total weight of 273g. Beyond its strength and durability, the stainless steel construction offers excellent fatigue life and enough resilience to be bent back into shape without cracking if it takes a hit out on the trail.

The XL combines thoughtful design, plenty of capacity, and a value-focused price, all while keeping production close to home Modelled after the original Fauna cargo cage, the XL is everything we’ve loved about Fauna so far, only bigger, bolder and ready for more.

Like the original, the XL Cargo Cage comes ready to mount with everything you need to get rolling. Each cage includes three M5x16 bolts and three TPU spacers, alongside the cage body and adjustable foot. It’s a straightforward package designed to make mounting simple and get your cargo secured without unnecessary fuss.

Get yours today at Fauna Components.

The post The Fauna XL Cargo Cage Is Here! appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: The New Repete G3:Verne
entry.content:
The Repete G3:Verne answers the age-old question every roadie has on a ride: “What is down that gravel road?” With clearance for 45mm tires, this made-in-the-Czech-Republic frame delivers light, fast, road-bike-like riding off-road. Read below for all the details.

Repete G3:Verne Quick Hits

  • Frame Material Columbus Spirit HSS | Hi-performance Omnicrom Steel Alloy
  • Fork Columbus Trefoil Allroad | 1 1/8″ – 1 1/2″ or ENVE All-Road In-Route 1 1/8″ – 1 1/2″
  • Headset IS52/28,6 – IS52/40
  • Dropouts Stainless Steel Dropouts | Flatmount | UDH
  • Head Tube Tapered | 1 1/8″ – 1 1/2″
  • Bottom Bracket Shell T47 – 68mm
  • Rear Dropouts Spacing 142×12 | M12x1 | 167,7mm
  • Front Dropouts Spacing 100×12 | M12x1,5 | E-thru
  • Max Rotor Size Rear 160mm | Front 160mm
  • Seatpost Diameter 31,6mm
  • Seat Clamp Diameter 34,9mm
  • Front Derailleur Clamp Diameter 34,9mm
  • Maximum Tire Clearance 700×45 (Columbus Trefoil Allroad) | 700×40 (ENVE All-Road In-Route)
  • Cable Routing Internal Routing | EPS, Di2 and eTap Compatible

Repete G3:Verne Overview

Czech bicycle manufacturer Repete introduces the new steel gravel model G3: Verne. Refining a concept proven over seven years of riding, the bike delivers what riders in this segment seek most: a balance between speed on tarmac and confidence on unpaved surfaces. The G3: Verne arrives with fully integrated cable routing, UDH standard compatibility, and continues to rely on precise handcraft in Prague.
The philosophy behind the G3: Verne is a lively ride character and responsive handling. The frame is purposefully optimized for tire widths from 35 to 45 mm. This choice made it possible to retain a shorter fork and chainstay length, keeping the G3: Verne’s geometry compact and agile. Rider feedback over recent years has clearly shown that a fast gravel bike — one that flies on the road while easily handling off-road terrain — is the most versatile category.

Repete Refined

The new G3 model brings significant visual and structural refinements. Following the brand’s road model R3: Reason, it features fully integrated cable routing through a shaped head tube with stainless steel cups (IS52/IS52 system). The frame is fully compatible with electronic groupsets including eTap, Di2, and EPS, forming a clean aesthetic unit with the fork.

Repete’s signature dropouts have been redesigned: they are now 3D-printed from stainless steel and fully support the UDH standard. This ensures effortless replacement part availability anywhere in the world, alongside direct Full Mount derailleur compatibility for maximum shifting precision.

Customers can choose between two internally routed carbon forks: the Columbus Trefoil Allroad (tire clearance up to 45 mm) or the ENVE All-Road In-Route (clearance up to 40 mm).

Frame Details and Finish Options

The frameset is available in three standard colors (Digger, Birch, Termix). Repete also offers custom paint options, with a palette ranging from pure pastel tones to distinctive shades inspired by the automotive world.

The frame is crafted from Columbus Spirit HSS high-strength chromoly steel (Omnicrom alloy). Triple-butted tubing with wall thicknesses down to just 0.4mm maximizes mechanical strength at the lowest possible weight. Steel naturally provides high ride comfort and vibration damping without material degradation or changes in characteristics over time. Rear-end comfort is further enhanced by flattened seatstays. Stiffness in the bottom bracket area is ensured by oversized tubing combined with a threaded T47 bottom bracket, which also guarantees simple servicing.

Made in the Czech Republic

All frames are built in Repete’s Prague workshop. The brand emphasizes in-house development of structural frame details and segments, collaborating closely with local Czech manufacturers for CNC machining, stainless steel and nylon 3D printing, and stainless steel casting.
Numbered Launch Edition: To celebrate the release of the G3: Verne, Repete has prepared a limited edition of 10 numbered frames. Customers ordering their frame from this edition directly via the Repete website receive a custom frameset color of their choice at no additional charge (400 EUR value).

See the new Repete R3:Verne.

The post The New Repete G3:Verne appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Tech Tidbits: Withings Adds $100/year Apple Health sync Fee, and Omata is Back!
entry.content:
Amidst what might end up being one of the more ‘robust’ weeks of the year in terms of new product announcements, I wanted to briefly mention/cover two items I thought were interesting.

Let’s get right into it, cause I’ve gotta get back outside capturing data!

Withings Adds $100/year Apple Health Fee:

I’m putting this solidly in the category of ‘Wait…what?’. In short, Withings, the maker of the original WiFi weight scale, and generally speaking one of the best bets for a mainstream weight scale, has decided that if you want to update your weight in Apple Health, it’s gonna cost you $99/year going forward. This ‘feature’ will now be rolled into their Withings+, which offers a bunch of other features that most weight scale purchasers simply don’t need.

In response to the backlash, Withings noted that:

A) This won’t apply to existing users, only new users from Oct 13th, 2026
B) That you can export your data to CSV or PDF, for free, as well as other 3rd-party sync integrations, which are free

The problem with CSV/PDF is that it’s virtually useless to end users. There is no standard ‘weight data format’. For the most part, anytime a company skips using an industry standard fitness format and instead says “Oh, we can export as CSV”, that’s a solid red flag for me. Sure, on the surface it sounds good. But in practice it’s just annoying AF.

The kicker is, Withings probably thought they were being clever here by announcing this before the holiday purchasing period, to capture new revenue there. And there’s no product in the sports tech landscape that seems more predictable in sales/discounts than Withings connected scales. Like clockwork around Black Friday, every…single…year.

Except the thing is, they screwed up and announced this annoying change too close to Black Friday. Now, it wouldn’t surprise me to see many tech sites out there that will caveat their Withings Black Friday deals. I certainly will. Which will drive users to the boatloads of even cheaper random connected scales that do nothing more than measure weight.

And as I’ve proven many times over, when it comes to basic weight measurement, even the cheapest scales on the market get it correct. Inversely, when it comes to body fat and BMI measurement, virtually no fancy scales are getting that right. Thus, if you just want weight, Withings is saying: “buy the cheaper competitor scales”.

After all, this connected scale here costs $20, has an astonishing 40,000 units per month sold on Amazon (I don’t think I’ve ever seen any electronic product that high before), and has 4.7/5.0 ratings. And of course, Apple Health integration is free (along with Google, Fitbit, etc.).

The same goes for this $34 travel weight scale that I use. It’s tiny, fits easily in the bottom of my suitcase without weighing much (~2 pounds/1kg), but still syncs to Apple Health and everything else on the planet. And the accuracy is spot-on with all the expensive scales I’ve tested.

Point being, Withings has long been the premium-priced scale with a few more bells and whistles, but moves like this will quickly alienate future buyers.

Omata is Back?

Silca has announced the acquisition of Omata and, with it, resumed sales of an updated Omata bike computer.

For those not familiar, nearly a decade ago I unboxed the Omata bike computer (photo above). It never ended up having a full review, as there was delay after delay in getting the software ready. And eventually, it fell by the wayside.

The gist of the Omata is that it’s a watch/gauge style bike commuter that simplifies things to just what you see on the display. Behind the scenes, it’s still recording extra data to review later and/or upload to Strava. Internally, it has GPS as well as Bluetooth & ANT+. So it can connect to power meters and heart rate sensors.

But in terms of what you see during the ride? Just three metrics:

– Distance
– Speed
– Ascent
– Time

It uses analog hands to do this, which are made in partnership with Seiko. Oh,  they’ve upgraded the charging to USB-C, which gets it about 17 hours of battery life.

The company says, though, that this batch is a “limited re-release” of the unit, though they don’t really say how limited that is. Unlike Withings above though, they do support industry-standard .FIT files, and can sync to various platforms/apps like most other bike computers. Note, though, that they are iOS-only, however, and don’t have an Android app.

The price is $800, which is obviously the most expensive bike computer on the market. You choose between two versions of it, seen below (Imperial and Metric):

You can head over to Silca’s site to enter your credit card.

While I think it looks really pretty on a shelf with other bike-themed things, it’s just not super practical out on the road for me. I want details like power and other metrics. But of course, there are plenty of people who prefer a more ‘minimalist’ experience – yet still want at least the core/basic metrics seen above.

—

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Suunto Race 3S In-Depth Review: A Pricey Upgrade
entry.content:
Suunto has just announced the new Suunto Race 3S, a small-form-factor watch that believes it needs a big-form-factor price increase. On top of that, Suunto has also launched a new subscription service, Suunto AI Coach, where new Suunto App features are being funneled into. I’ve been using the Suunto Race 3S over the last few weeks, and in this review I’ll dive into how it all works, and whether Suunto can justify the price.

The new Suunto Race 3S includes a brighter display, more storage, and some software feature updates that the existing Race S didn’t get this past summer. This isn’t really a major change from the previous model, but nonetheless these updates are appreciated. It also features upgraded materials, shifting from a stainless steel bezel to a titanium bezel.

In any case, I’ve been putting it through its paces over the last little bit, across all sorts of activities to see how it holds up, and how it compares to other newly announced watches from the last few weeks.

With that, let’s dive right into it!

What’s New:

Now, as you probably know, the Suunto Race 3S is an upgrade to the existing Suunto Race S. There was no Suunto Race 2S, and equally confusingly, there is no larger Suunto Race 3 companion at this point. When I asked about the Suunto Race 3 elephant in the room, Suunto simply said a variant of ‘No comment’. Thus, that elephant will stay with us for now, joining other elephants I’ll talk about later.

Of course, when you look at changes vs. the original Suunto Race S, that watch continued to get meaningful firmware updates until this past April. So I’ll ignore all of those things and focus on the new stuff otherwise (software and hardware).

Starting off with the hardware changes:

– Upgraded peak display brightness from 1,000 nits to 2,000 nits
– Upgraded lens cover material from Gorilla Glass to Sapphire Crystal glass
– Updated bezel material from stainless steel to titanium
– Upgraded optical heart rate sensor
– Faster processor (Apollo 510)
– Increased GPS time from 30 hours to 38 hours (dual-frequency), 45 hours (single-frequency)
– Increased smartwatch daily battery life from 9 days to 12 days
– Increased internal storage from 32GB to 64GB
– Added support for offline music playback (MP3 files, no streaming services)
– Increased number of SuuntoPlus apps in a single profile from 2 to 3
– Slightly increased official case size from 45mm to 46mm
– Decreased weight from 60g to 56g
– Increased retail price from $349USD to $599USD (and 349EUR to 499EUR)

Do note that while you might see NFC listed on some spec sheets, that’s only applicable for the China market. There’s no contactless payment integration elsewhere. Unfortunately, like the music streaming services piece, those industry gates closed a decade ago.

Then there are a few new software features, mainly ones that rolled out on the Suunto Race 2 this past summer:

– Added Tide Widget
– Expanded map labels (road names, water, mountain peaks)
– Added Ascent as an exercise target

Finally, Suunto has noted that there’s a new ‘Race Planner’ feature coming later this year to the Suunto Race 3S, though it’s not there at launch. Here’s a quick blurb on that:

This sounds super interesting, and so I’m keen to see how this works. Especially the pieces looking at weather. For example, does that also look at your historical training weather (e.g., if you train in cold temps, but then arrive at a hot-temp race day). And, best of all, it doesn’t require Suunto AI Coach.

Finally, when it comes to model colors, here are those three options – purple, white, and black:

With that, let’s get into the box.

In the box:

This section is pretty straightforward. Above is the Suunto Race 3S box, following the same design as other recent Suunto watches.

Below are the contents of said box:

You’ve got the band/strap, the pod (separated from the band), the braided charging cable, and some paper stuff.

The charging cable follows other recent Suunto models, and is magnetic and much better than the one that came with the original Suunto S model, which I found would often become misaligned.

In any case, you simply embark on a 10-15-second IKEA assembly project to attach the standard band straps to the watch pod, and you’re off and running.

The Basics:

In this section, I’m going to look at some of the basics of the watch, including daily usage such as activity tracking, sleep, etc. As well as pieces like responsiveness and general usability.

The Suunto Race 3S has a three-button layout, as well as a touchscreen. You can mostly use either touch or buttons for navigating around the user interface. The upper right button accesses the sport menu, the middle Digital Crown allows access to pinned widgets during smartwatch use (and of course scrolls up/down), and the bottom button acts as a back/escape button.

The left side has no buttons. Meanwhile, the touchscreen is a 2,000-nit display that’s perfectly viewable in both bright sunny conditions or shade conditions. I live on a Mediterranean island, and I’ve had no issues viewing the display in any scenarios out on the trails. Oh, for fun, here are three watches side-by-side: Suunto Race S, Suunto Race 2, and Suunto Race 3S

That said, it can’t be left unstated that virtually all watches released in 2026 are using 3,000-nit panels. The COROS Pace 4 Pro released a few weeks ago is using a 3,500-nit display (which is also larger), and atop that, the more-capable watch is $150 cheaper. To be super clear here, I have no issue with seeing the display at all. Period, hard-stop. However, we can’t ignore the fact that Suunto is putting in kinda old tech but with over-the-top premium prices. To me, the ‘savings’ on this display panel should be reflected in the price. It’s clearly not.

The only minor ‘nit’-picking I’d have with the display is that their power-saving algorithms seem a little bit aggressive at times, quickly dimming the panel within a few seconds of wrist-raise. Again, the display is still visible, but this could use a bit of work.

Speaking of brightness, note that for whatever weird reason, there’s no physical LED flashlight like there is in the Suunto Vertical 2 watch (which is priced the same at $599). You still have a screen-based flashlight, but obviously that’s not the same.

Perhaps given Suunto’s lawsuit with Garmin concerning the topic, they got a bit skittish. Either way, it’s a bit of a bummer.

In any case, scrolling down into the widgets, you’ve got a customizable set of quick-access data bits. I will note that if you watch the video, you’ll see it’s more laggy here than the older Suunto Race S – despite the claims of a faster processor. This is such a good example of why processor specs mean absolutely nothing in most devices. You can have the fastest processor in the world, but if the firmware/operating system isn’t optimized for it, it’ll still be slower than an optimized processor. Again, check out the above video for that.

As for those widgets, they all work just as before. Aside from the new Tides one, there’s nothing new here. You can tap into any given smaller widget in this list to open up details about that topic, such as steps, sleep, weather, etc.

When it comes to things like sleep tracking, the times I went to sleep and woke up have largely been correct here, usually matching the other wearables within a few minutes. The same goes for the HRV status values. I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Meanwhile, most of the data around heart rate-driven metrics comes from the new optical heart rate sensor seen on the bottom. As I’ll show you within the accuracy section, this heart rate sensor is a huge jump up over the previous Suunto Race S sensor, which wasn’t super awesome.

Speaking of other internal-ish things, the unit now has 64GB of internal storage, which is ostensibly mostly for offline music (yes, it’s also for maps, but Suunto’s maps are so well optimized that you simply don’t need anywhere near that much storage…more on that in the next section).

Now, with Suunto’s offline music playback, it requires you to transfer MP3 files via USB cable to the device. There are no offline streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), and that’s simply not going to happen anytime soon. Those industry gates closed nearly a decade ago now, and the only way Suunto would gain access to them is by going back to WearOS. Nonetheless, if you’re one of 12 people who are still transferring your owned/“borrowed” MP3 files to your watch via cable, you can do that here. You’ll pair up any Bluetooth audio device (e.g., headphones) to the watch, and off you go. It all worked pretty easily for me, and you can also load in playlists as well.

Finally, when it comes to smartphone notifications, you’ll get the basic text and emoji from your phone.

Ok, with all that sorted, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports Usage & Mapping:

Next up, we’ve got all things sports, including mapping and navigation.

To access a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button, which opens up the workout panel. Here it’ll automatically open your last sport mode, and start searching for GPS (if outside), as well as get heart rate lock. Further, if you’ve got paired sensors (like cycling sensors or an external heart rate sensor), it’ll pair to those too.

You can change the sport mode to one of a boatload of other sport modes in the list:

Back on that main page though, you can select to load a course (within Navigation), as well as select/load SuuntoPlus apps. The Suunto Race 3S supports up to three concurrent enabled SuuntoPlus apps within a given sport profile (you can have additional apps loaded but not enabled). In addition, you can also load up ‘Guides’, which would include things like structured workouts. However, you can only load two apps + one concurrent guide, if using guides.

Finally, there are also the exercise options, where you can tweak various display, map, and other target settings. For example, the Suunto Race 3S added the ability to set an Ascent target (similar to how you might set a calorie or distance target). This came in a firmware update for other newer Suunto watches this summer, but the existing Suunto Race S was skipped.

In any case, circling back, I’m gonna add a course to navigate for my trail run. So I’ll select that back in the Navigation/Routes area:

In terms of maps, the Suunto Race 3S doesn’t have any maps pre-loaded, though they are easily downloadable via WiFi from Suunto. You simply go into the app and choose the regions you want. Here are some random sizes to get a feel for things:

Since I’m here, one thing I really wish Suunto would sort out is their app to watch syncing/configuration situation. For years it’s been that as soon as the watch thinks you want to tweak something, it starts syncing, which in turn prohibits you from actually tweaking the thing until it’s done, taking forever to do that. It’s just very 1990s-modal style. I can’t think of a single other wearable device that still has that restriction left. And more critically, there’s no way to cancel the app from syncing once it starts. That’d at least half-way solve it.

It’s in this area of the app that you’d modify things like the data fields/pages of your sport modes, add new SuuntoPlus apps, create interval workouts, and more. Of course, like in the past, you still can’t modify default sports profiles; you have to create a new custom one if you want to tweak something. And it needs to sync a bunch back and forth too. These are the types of actual useful things I wished Suunto would focus on, rather than adding offline MP3 music support that virtually nobody will use.

With that all sorted, synced, and re-synced, we’re ready to start our workout. Off I go for a run. While running, I’ll of course see my data pages as configured:

From a navigation standpoint, I’ll get a little chirp and then an on-screen notification when a turn comes up. And then if I miss a turn, I’ll get a notification about that too, such as this:

Otherwise, the route shows as expected, and in terms of the responsiveness of the map, it’s a double-edged sword. For rotation, things were instant, and I didn’t experience any black square tiles. You can see this in the video.

But for zooming in/out, there was always at least a second or two of black square tiles. Ironically, a runner friend was with me as I was sitting there filming this, and not being familiar with Suunto watches, he was a bit surprised and asked “Is that normal?”

And ultimately, different companies handle things in different ways. For Garmin, when it slow-map renders, it has a fuzzy look or other color-matching tiles (or shows a tile at a higher zoom level first, before enumerating the detailed tile). Most other companies do the same. But in Suunto’s case, they’re just showing black tiles, which looks a bit sloppy.

Even more so, because I’d also notice these tiles as I run, if I had the map screen just open. Meaning, visible at a glance on my wrist even when not fully raised. Again, we can have an academic debate on slow-map-loading differences (more detail vs less detail, etc.), but I think we can all agree that the black tiles just look rough.

In any case, you’ll also be able to see your progress on the elevation and climbs, both for the full course, and then specific climbs as you trip them:

All of this worked perfectly fine. After the workout, you’ll get a summary of your workout as expected on the watch:

And then likewise you’ll see the additional detail within the Suunto App:

Assuming you have your account connected to one of Suunto’s boatload of partners (e.g., Strava, TrainingPeaks, etc.), it’ll automatically push that data off to those platforms. Again, all of that worked without issue for me.

So then, let’s talk about the accuracy of that data.

Accuracy of Heart Rate & GPS:

The new Suunto Race 3S has a new optical heart rate sensor compared to the existing Suunto Race S. Suunto says this new sensor has six LEDs and four photodetectors behind 2.5D curved sensor glass. No matter what it has behind it, I’ll just state things up front: It’s really darn good in my testing.

I’ll also cover the GNSS/GPS side of things, as well as battery and elevation bits down below. But the GNSS piece hasn’t changed here, so we’ll keep that efficient.

Let’s start off with this slightly hilly run I did. It started off with a long and occasionally steep descent, before some flats, and then going all the way back up again. As a reminder, hills (going down), can often be challenging for optical HR sensors. Still, the Suunto nailed it here. I’ve got zero complaints.

Next, we’ve got a 90-minute long trail run across plenty of varied terrain (steep stuff, shallow stuff, rocking spicy stuff, etc.). And again, overall very good.

About the only thing I could nitpick here is this section for about 20 seconds, where it’s off by about 3-5bpm. That’s nothing in a 98-minute long workout. Again, really good job here.

Here’s another trail run from yesterday. Setting aside whatever happened with the chest strap at the 28-minute marker for a few seconds, things here were quite good as well. Again, there’s virtually nothing to be upset about, and this also included some steep ups/downs.

Next, just for fun, check out this shorter morning gravel ride thing I did a few days ago. I was taking photos and such on this ride of a few different devices. So lots of stop-and-go. Lots of pretty spicy typical Mallorca gravel chunk (most would call it MTB material). And yet, it absolutely nails this. Like, really solid job while cycling.

Now, I’m going to continue to test this sensor, but switch over to the new Suunto Run 2 sensor over the coming weeks, so stay tuned for that. I don’t expect a difference though. Either way, this represents a major improvement for Suunto over past sensors.

Meanwhile, on the GPS side, let’s quickly run through some of these. Here’s that city run from a few nights ago. At a high level, obviously all look pretty good.

Meanwhile, in the actual city/downtown parts with tall buildings, none of the units did amazing. None were bad, but across the board (Garmin, Suunto, Apple), all of them were ‘blah’ accuracy-wise. I’m not quite sure why.

You can see this here as well. Again, nothing was crazy-bad, but all four units took turns crashing through buildings slightly, cutting corners, and generally acting like the drunk tourists that fill this area.

That said, as soon as I left the buildings behind, it was perfectly fine on the rest of the run:

Moving along, looking at yesterday’s trail run, which includes cliffs, ravines, trees, etc., things at a high level look good:

I could quibble about each unit being a few meters offset at different parts of the route. Here the Fenix 9 Pro briefly goes across the road, then the COROS and Suunto do the same some 20 seconds later.

Still, we’re talking less than a 5-meter difference in most cases, such as this here:

Or going around this gate for cars. The Garmin & Suunto were most correct here; the COROS went a bit more lazily around it.

Anyway, this is the pattern over and over again – basically all these units were spot on across runs, rides, etc. I’ve got some actual swim tests to do this weekend (I’ve spent a bunch of time in the water swimming with it, but wasn’t doing accuracy testing).

As for looking at the elevation, no major concerns on any of my activities. Here’s that 90-minute trail run:

This is the one I showed the other day in the Garmin MARQ Gen3 review, where for some reason both Garmin units started sliding downwards while I stood and took some photos (27min marker). Garmin’s already digging into it, as it’s likely firmware-related if two different units do it. I will say there’s a little bit of separation early on in the above that seems a bit odd between the Suunto/COROS and the Apple/Garmin watches. Though those all eventually bundled back up together again.

As for the battery bits, here’s the official battery chart:

Looking at my battery life in always-on display, with roughly 60-90mins of GPS time per day, I’m closer to about 5ish days, maybe a touch bit more, but a little shy of the 7-day above (which is spec’d as 60mins per day, versus my times a bit higher). Also, my routes had navigation enabled, which would draw more battery.

Speaking of which, looking at that 98-minute trail run, you can see it burned about 5%, putting me on a 28-hour battery estimate in dual-frequency/multiband mode. This is a touch bit lower than the always-on specs above, but again remember I did have navigation enabled, which draws more battery.

Also, kudos to Suunto for including battery data in their .FIT files (Garmin, Wahoo, and others do so, though unfortunately COROS does not).

In any case, in terms of all my accuracy bits, I’m good across the board here; I’ve got no concerns in any category. Again, for the heart rate sensor side, this is a big upgrade.

Suunto AI Coach Subscription:

Next, Suunto has announced a new Suunto AI Coach subscription feature, which let’s you use your current and historical Suunto data to get race planning information and tons more. This feature is launching on/with the Suunto Race 3S, though it is expected to go to other watch user bases. It’s currently fully on the app itself, as there’s no on-device component.

Suunto has a pretty good 10-minute video that explains the boatload of features that exist there.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

My one (kinda big) quibble here is that Suunto Race 3S users get 3 months free to the service, yet Suunto hasn’t defined what said service will actually cost once that free trial ends. And somehow that rubs me the wrong way. Perhaps it’s because my inbox is filled with AI vibe-coded slop apps that often attempt to hook you into the platform before eventually charging you down the road. In this case, Suunto is clear they’ll be charging you eventually, but aren’t saying what that is. Thus, once you get hooked on it, you’ll feel compelled to start paying for it.

Now mind you, what Suunto is offering certainly seems a heck of a lot more compelling than what Amazfit, Garmin, and others are doing. It doesn’t seem as deep as what Fitbit/Google are doing, but again, we don’t know Suunto’s pricing yet. Suunto says that part of the reason they haven’t decided pricing is because they want to see what people actually use, and get feedback. Which is fair enough, but still seems like something they could have done before they launched it.

Now, despite my annoyance with Suunto’s AI Coach rollout, I will give them all the credit in the world that they’ve also announced a new Suunto MCP that’ll be free for all Suunto users. This joins COROS in offering such a thing for free. I have a feeling we’re going to see similar announcements in the near future from others. Note that in the case of Suunto’s MCP, the details are thin at this point, other than it’ll be free, and it’ll exist. Still, I take both of those for the moment.

Wrap-Up:

Suunto has had a string of solid product launches over the last couple of years, paired with frequent and meaningful firmware/feature updates on the app side. And good expansion on the developer side. They’ve been on a roll across the board. But I struggle to put the Suunto Race 3S in that category of wins. This watch feels…off.

To begin, the biggest issue is the price. At $599USD/499EUR, it’s more than a 70% USD price increase over the launch price of the Suunto Race S just two years ago. And it’s not like they’ve drastically changed the hardware. Sure, it has a brighter 2,000-nit display panel, but that panel is what other companies were putting in their watches two years ago, not the 3,000-3,500-nit panels that companies are putting in watches in 2026. Further, while they increased the storage from 32GB to 64GB, it doesn’t really serve any meaningful purpose. Suunto’s maps are tiny in size, and easily fit within even just 16GB of space. And while in theory the extra space is for music playback, the reality is virtually nobody is downloading MP3s to their watches in 2026 (since Suunto doesn’t support offline music from any streaming service). Plus, where are the other hardware features that other companies are putting in their watches for half the price (e.g., flashlights, voice, microphone & proper speaker, etc.)?

After a string of wins, I think Suunto missed the boat on this one. It feels both overpriced, and kinda seems like it’s just a collection of leftover hardware parts, rather than representing the start of a new Race 3 series generation of watches. Perhaps if it was priced at $399 or at most $449, I’d feel differently. But with the just-released COROS Pace 4 Pro being at $449, that’s a very tough spot for Suunto to be competing in with the specs they have in the Race 3S.

With that, thanks for reading.

entry.title: Garmin MARQ Gen3 In-Depth Review: Worth $3,100?
entry.content:
The first thing to understand about Fight Club…err…MARQ Club, is that it’s oddly not about the price. Nor is it supposed to be a classical timepiece meant to hand down to your grandchildren. Just like people who buy a business class ticket across the Atlantic for 7 hours of flying at $4,000 don’t pass that down to their grandchildren in 20 years.

But more importantly, the second thing to understand about MARQ Club is that for the first time ever, the MARQ actually has a slate of new features and additional hardware that the Fenix doesn’t. Up till now, the MARQ series (and Chronos before it in 2016) was simply a ‘swankier’ Fenix. But it never had any truly unique hardware or features (save getting JetLag software features just barely earlier back in 2022). But certainly not unique hardware components. That pattern ends now, with Garmin giving a good technical reason to ‘upsell’ the MARQ. This comes in the form of real-time ClimbPro *without* having loaded a course. Both for running/hiking/walking, as well as cycling. That’s a first, not just for Garmin, but for any company to have route-less automatic ClimbPro. And Garmin has added additional features beyond that. But, again, more details in a second.

And ultimately, testing out these features and how the watch works day in and day out is what I’m here for. I’ve been testing both the new MARQ Gen3 Diver unit and the MARQ Gen3 Adventurer unit across a boatload of different activities. No really, an actual literal boatload. Boats were involved. Many times. Plus of course, things like running, cycling, diving, gym workouts, swimming, and plenty more.

Note that these two units are media loaner units. Also note that Garmin did hold a media event in Mallorca last month, though since I live in Mallorca I actually pedaled 15 minutes to said event and then changed in the parking lot, James Bond style. Point is, I didn’t take any money for travel or accommodations there, as always. I’m just gonna tell it like it is – the good, bad, and ugly. Though honestly, there’s not a lot of ugly here.

With that, let’s get right into it!

What’s New:

Comparing the MARQ Gen3 to the previous MARQ Gen2 is a bit overwhelming because the previous Gen2 unit was from 2022, and was essentially an Epix (non-Pro). In between now and then, there have been four iterations, once per year: Epix Pro, Fenix 8, Fenix 8 Pro, and now the Fenix 9. The MARQ Gen3 is based on the Fenix 9 series.

Thus, if I were to combine all of my ‘What’s New’ lists, it’d be hundreds upon hundreds of lines long to cover all the features. Instead, I want to focus on the biggest-ticket items if you were coming from a MARQ Gen2. Then below that, the things that are unique going from the new Fenix 9 to the new MARQ Gen3 models. Make sense?

First, here are the biggest ticket items compared from MARQ Gen2 to MARQ Gen3:

– Upgraded 1.4” AMOLED display at 3,000 nits
– Fully borderless display design (meaning, no extra space between display and ceramic bezel)
– Added three-color LED flashlight to front of the unit
– Added LTE communication features (calling, texting, LiveTrack, etc.)
– Added satellite messaging features (for non-cellular areas, such as texting, Emergency SOS, weather)
– Added full scuba diving and free diving features (unit is fully depth-gauge certified to 40m)
– Added microphone and full speaker support, including voice assistant, voice control, voice notes, phone calls from wrist, music playback via speaker, and more
– Added Gen5 optical heart rate sensor, including medically certified ECG & Afib detection
– Added all the Fenix 9 Software features, including Garmin Epic features, indoor rowing connectivity/features, Rucking expansion, Stamina features, Ski Erg features, Field Tools, and plenty more
– Added all the Fenix 8 Pro software features, including custom focus modes, calculator app, Evening Report feature, Running Economy, Running Tolerance, and numerous other Running & Triathlon Features
– Added all the Fenix 8 software features, including the new Fenix user interface, and eventually some months later a boatload of sport modes via firmware updates
– Added all the Epix Pro software features, including Endurance Score, Hill Score, shaded relief on maps, 30+ new sport profiles, faster charging speeds, RedShift mode, multiband GNSS/GPS
– Has full offline mapping and navigation features globally

From an LTE & Satellite messaging features standpoint, all of the following are included in all MARQ Gen3 units (unless sold in a country that doesn’t permit it):

– LTE Live two-way voice calls
– LTE LiveTrack (30-second sampling rate)
– LTE Voice Messaging
– LTE Text Messaging
– LTE Weather
– LTE & Satellite Emergency SOS
– LTE Location Check-Ins
– LTE Incident Detection & Assistance
– Satellite Messaging (basic texting)
– Satellite position/location check-ins
– Satellite Emergency SOS (via Garmin Response)
– Satellite updating of weather (new in the Fenix 9 Pro)

As I said, there’s just a ton of new features here. Next, and perhaps of more interest to folks, are the differences between the Fenix 9 Pro inReach to MARQ Gen 3?

In other words, you’re paying an extra few thousand dollars; aside from all the fancy/premium materials, what else do you get?

– Upgraded 128GB of internal storage (versus 64GB on the Fenix 9 series)
– Added Worldwide Topographic maps pre-loaded (Fenix 9 is essentially your local continent, and the rest you download as needed)
– Added on-device real-time ClimbPro for pedestrian & cycling activities *WITHOUT* a route loaded (Fenix 9 requires a course)
– Added on-device address navigation such as 123 Maple Street (the Fenix 9 can go to POI, but not an address)
– Added Predictive search via the keyboard showing suggestions
– Added Lume Mode, mimicking night lume on a watch
– Added slate of MARQ-only watch faces, including unique calendar ones
– Expanded use of ‘Styles’ feature, increasing customization of watch faces
– Expanded color scheme option, increasing color scheme of watch faces
– All the individual watch vertical features (e.g., flying features for the Aviator unit, extra diving features for Diver, etc.)

Of note for the real-time ClimbPro piece, a big part of why they have the extra storage is to enable this scenario. In order to pull this off, they have to pre-cache all of these climbs, which is a mind-boggling amount of pre-caching. We see that today on the cycling-only side within the Garmin Edge units. But obviously once you add every tiny goat-path of a trail out there in the world, that gets massive.

The only downside is that at present that feature has been slightly delayed, and isn’t yet available for me to test. It sounds like this is a matter of days away, and not months or such. I’ll update things accordingly here, once that happens.

Next, there are a few super-specific hardware differences, aside from all the premium materials, that I want to call out:

– The buttons on MARQ have actual mechanical clicking, while still being induction buttons for waterproof reasons. This is different from the Fenix 9, where the buttons are induction, and the ‘click’ is done through the vibration motor. Here, it’s actually a mechanical system outside the case of the watch, within the button.

Also, here you can see the sealed case design of MARQ Gen3 (and Fenix 9):

– All MARQ units have a full ceramic bezel, and within that, the coloring is ‘baked’ all the way through. Meaning, on the Diver, for example, the blue you see is actually fully blue, so even if it scratches, it’s still blue. The white lettering you see (in the case of Diver) is etched out, and then filled with ink.
– The MARQ Gen3 series has a different charging cable. It’s a magnetic one that snaps to the back of the unit. It’s different than the also-unique MARQ Gen2 cable, because the optical HR sensor and case design are different, and wouldn’t have been compatible.  Oh, and it’s a braided cable.
– All MARQ units except the Athlete also get a secondary silicone band in the box, for athletic wear (e.g., to not have substantial water damage to the leather band). The Athlete edition is already such a band.

Ok, now, there are also per-model unique things, but the above covers the across-the-board changes. With that, let’s dive into the models.

The Models – An Overview

Next up are all the models. I know this section might be a bit long, but we’re ultimately talking about six different models. Each of these models aligns to a different top-end unit within the Garmin watch lineup. For example, Golfer aligns to Garmin’s Approach lineup. Commander aligns to the Tactix lineup, Aviator to D2 Mach, Diver to Quatix/Descent, and Athlete/Adventurer to Fenix.

Here are the MARQ Gen3 models and their pricing:

MARQ Athlete: $2,500USD/2,550EUR

MARQ Adventurer: $2,700USD/2,750EUR

MARQ Golfer: $2,800USD/2,850EUR

MARQ Diver: $3,100USD/3,150EUR

MARQ Commander: $3,100USD/3,150EUR

MARQ Aviator: $3,100USD/3,150EUR

Note that, as a quick starting-point reminder, all units:

– Have a full Grade 5 titanium case (which is harder than the Fenix 9 titanium level, which is Grade 2)
– Have a full ceramic bezel
– Have both induction-sealed buttons (the case has no holes for the buttons), as well as full tactical mechanical click
– All watch faces are available to all MARQ models

With that, let’s get straight into each model and some additional details.

MARQ Athlete:

This is effectively the ‘base’ model, and it essentially has the same software features as a Garmin Fenix 9 series, plus the extra MARQ things noted above. But it doesn’t have other-category extra features like you’ll see on the Aviator (flying) or Golfer (golfing) models.

Still, there are some hardware differences here:

– $2,500USD/2,550EUR
– It’s a full titanium case
– Your VO2Max & Recovery Time are shown on the bezel, in the upper left/bottom left, tied to the watch face
– It has so-called ‘AMP Yellow’ accents
– It has the integrated silicone band

I’ve gotta say, I just wish this model was prettier. Or more specifically, didn’t have yellow on it. I get that’s a personal choice (in the same way I like the orange accents on Fenix). But to me, the yellow just feels kinda dated here. But again, my wife would argue my fashion trends are often dated as well. Still, I sometimes feel like the point of the Athlete model is to convince you to buy a better-looking MARQ model.

MARQ Adventurer

Meanwhile, over to the Adventurer, this one might be my favorite-looking model, tied with the Diver. On the regular though, I think the Adventurer is where I’d be if I were to sacrifice a few years of ice cream budget for a MARQ watch.

Like the Athlete model, this unit doesn’t have any specific extra software features over an existing Fenix 9 Pro inReach; instead, it’s still about materials.

– $2,700USD/2,750EUR
– Has a 360-degree compass on bezel
– Has a sunburst brushing effect on bezel
– Has machined notches for N/S/E/W marking on bezel
– Has micro-knurled buttons
– Band is vegetable-tanned Italian full-grain leather on the outside, but has an HNBR hybrid strap on the backside to minimize against light sweat damaging the leather

I’ve been using this model for my dryer actives, occasionally switching to the silicone band for any sweatier activities. I was kinda curious how far I could push the hybrid band piece. In my case, I did two workouts with the leather/hybrid band. One was an easy 90-minute trail run on a windy day where basically I was sweating, but not massively so. Still, after that I could see some slight areas of color change on the band.

I think this is where, once you had a bit more light sweat, the whole band would be the same darker leather color and life is grand again.

Meanwhile, I did an hour or so gravel bike ride where it was low intensity, and no negative change there. As Garmin noted, long-term with occasional rain or such, this would probably age quite nicely. Otherwise, I’d switch to the silicone strap for other workouts.

MARQ Golfer:

Next is the Golfer edition; this ‘Pine Green’ color scheme unit aligns most closely to the features of the Approach S72 unit, though minus two features that require additional hardware. From a MARQ hardware standpoint, notable differences here are:

– $2,800USD/2,850EUR
– 18-hole indicator in white detailing on bezel (aligned with software in the display)
– White detailing on the buttons
– Jacquard woven tri-color band/strap
– Ceramic end links
– All Approach S72 Software features including Virtual Caddie, Putt Break, and Biometric data aligned to each shot on the hole (e.g., first shot vs at the hole, vs transition between holes). However, it does not have the S72 ‘Swing Metrics’ and ‘Driving Range Mode’ features, as those require additional hardware.

MARQ Aviator:

This model aligns with Garmin’s D2 Mach 2 unit in terms of software features. From a hardware standpoint, this unit has:

– $3,100USD/3,150EUR
– Mirror-polished black ceramic bezel
– 24-hour UTC on outside of bezel, they selected UTC vs GMT, as aviation uses UTC
– Italian calfskin padded leather strap
– Strap has a deployant clasp system
– All software features from the D2 Mach 2, including full aviation airspace maps, avionics connectivity to Garmin cockpit systems, Morning Report with flight conditions integration (including IFR condition states).

MARQ Diver:

This watch replaces what was the MARQ Captain last time, focused purely on boating. Now with diving being part of all MARQ editions, the MARQ Diver is a bit of a blend between the Garmin Descent product and Garmin Quatix products, but in MARQ form. The difference though, is that this doesn’t have the added wireless air integration on the dive side that the Descent products have, but it does have the DiveView maps, as well as all the boating bits from a Quatix series device.

Additionally, the following notes:

– $3,100USD/3,150EUR
– 60-minute (up to) quick timer on watch face
– Silicone dive bracelet with deployment clasp and 15mm micro adjustment
– Has Dive Readiness feature
– Has NDL Aware Depth Metrics
– Has Apnea Hunt Mode
– Has Gauge Mode
– Has full global DiveView maps (including depth and dive sites)
– All Quatix Sailing & Boating features except the ‘Boat Mode’ (which is different than the Boat profile, as Boat Mode essentially does some prioritization pieces with the settings).
– Has boating/marine Autopilot Heading hold (with compatible Garmin boat equipment)

This is the second model that I used, mainly when diving as well as out boating. I’ve got more thoughts on that down below. Do note, though, that from a dive functionality standpoint, outside of the added DiveView maps, all of the MARQ units otherwise have the same dive features, as those come from the Fenix 9 series (well technically, started with the Fenix 8 series).

As I noted earlier, this would probably be a close tie for my next-favorite unit in terms of color scheme. It looks really nice out on the water, or even with the right outfit. Obviously, given the blue look, it won’t be for everyone, but dang, it really shines when the light hits it right.

MARQ Commander:

The unit is essentially taking the Tactical features from the Garmin Tactix series watches, and then blending them into a Fenix 9 variant. As with the Quatix and D2 pilot series, there aren’t yet Fenix 9 variants of those watches or the existing Tactix watches. So this is filling the gap at the high-end price point.

Here are the differences:

– $3,100USD/3,150EUR
– Matte carbon gray DLC bezel (no polished or glossy surfaces)
– 24-hour UTC Military Time Bezel etchings
– Jacquard woven camouflage 3-color weave pattern
– Has all Tactix 8 tactical features, including: Applied Ballistics Solver, Stealth Mode, Night Vision Compatible, Xero C2 Compatibility, Stealth Mode, and Kill Switch (which purges data)

I did actually wear this one for about half a day. As with most Garmin Tactix watches, this one kinda depends on what you’re looking for.

This one stands out the least out of the group in terms of the ‘swankiness’ of it. It feels very understated, to the point that I’m not entirely convinced most people would realize it’s a $3,000 watch. Obviously there are some very nice touches, such as the Jacquard woven strap, but again, to each their own.

The Box:

Here’s just a quick look at the box itself. This is a bit of a ‘step down’ from some of the metallic boxes of the past, though Garmin basically said that folks found the past packaging a bit wasteful. This one finds a good balance between being quite elegant, but also totally recyclable.

Inside the box you’ll essentially find your watch, the extra silicone band for sports (except in the Athlete model), the braided charging cable, and then some paper stuffs you won’t read.

Speaking of which, here’s that charging cable:

And you can see how it snaps on:

The simple reason you don’t see this for every Garmin device, is that each device would require a different charging cable for each case design, including optical HR sensor bump, etc.

With that, let’s get into basic usage.

The Basics:

In this section, I’m going to run through the general basics of the MARQ Gen3 unit. This applies to all the MARQ Gen3 models and is virtually identical to that of the Fenix 9 units. Thus, I’ll do a bit of a truncated version of my deeper ‘Basics’ section found on my recent Fenix 9 In-Depth Review here.

Starting off with the user interface, the MARQ uses the standard Garmin 5-button layout, in combination with a full touchscreen. As with other Garmin touchscreen devices, you can choose whether or not you want the touch enabled at both a system level, as well as a per sport level (for example, perhaps not while sailing, but you do want it for running).

The screen on the MARQ is a 1.4” 3,000-nit AMOLED display, and is 36% larger than the Gen2 MARQ, and 2.5X brighter than the Gen2 MARQ. It’s also a fully borderless display, whereas the Fenix 9 series has a secondary border between the display and the bezel. As one who lives on a sunny Mediterranean island, I have had zero issues seeing the display in the brightest of sunny days on the water. And inversely, no issues with the display at night.

In fact, speaking of at night, if enabled (it’s off by default), you can have the watch emulate a lume mode. This can be enabled in the Display settings (same place as Color Shift), and can be either automatic at a certain time (such as 2 hours before bedtime, or after sunset), or just manually enabled.

Personally, I don’t find this look super awesome. But again, as with most style things, to each their own. I find the stock watch faces so good, that this kinda kills the vibe a bit. As a reminder, it’s not on by default.

Anyway, as noted there’s a bunch of watch faces you can choose from.

Additionally, for each watch face, there are additional styling and color options you can set:

Next, down from there are all your widgets and widget glances. You can customize which ones to display and the ordering. The world is your oyster here. Within that, you can open any given widget for more details about the metrics behind it. This could be steps, sleep, barometric altimeter, Training Load, Training Readiness, or many other metrics.

All of this information is of course synced to Garmin Connect, Garmin’s cloud platform, as well as the mobile app. You can access it on your smartphone, or a desktop computer. By default, your watch will sync via Bluetooth to your phone. But it can also sync via both WiFi or USB cable.
