The MARQ supports smartphone notifications like most other wearables, and on Android you can do basic replies as well as see photos/images sent to your phone (on your watch). Whereas on iOS, you can’t yet reply to messages (due to historical Apple limitations), nor can you see images yet. Though those restrictions have recently eased in the EU, so perhaps soon it’ll be enabled on Garmin devices.

In terms of battery life, you’re going to see similar stats to the Garmin Fenix 9 series for the 47mm units. Thus, in my case, I’ve been getting roughly 4-6 days of battery for the units I’ve been using, in an always-on display configuration with 1-2 hours of GPS time per day on average. If you turn on gesture-based display (which is the default, btw), then you’re likely going to get 2-3x the battery life, up to about 15 days of battery between charges.

Finally, all MARQ Gen3 units now have an LED flashlight. In this case, it’s the same trim-color flashlight just launched on the Fenix 9, which includes a white LED at four brightness levels, and then a red and green LED mode. This is a real LED on the front of the unit:

And the throw of the light is roughly the same as a smartphone flashlight. Now flashlights on the front of watches might sound a bit Inspector Gadgety, but as any Garmin owner will (happily) tell you, it’s a game changer for just silly night tasks. Sure, you can use it in a tent on the side of a cliff. But it’s simply just something I use every night for getting something in a kid’s room in the middle of the night, getting around an unknown hotel room at 3AM, or finding something under a couch.

Ok, with that, we’ve got a lot to cover, so let’s shift into some of the sports features.

Sports Features:

Next up, I’m going to do a quick look at the sporting features. Keeping in mind that, again, this is a full Garmin Fenix, which is typically considered Garmin’s flagship sport watch, and is further considered the most in-depth sports watch on the market today. Even Garmin’s competitors wouldn’t try to argue that.

As with the previous section, I go even deeper on this in my Fenix 9 in-depth review (breaking out bits like mapping, navigation, training load, etc.). But for here, we’ll keep things a bit more streamlined.

To access a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button, which opens up the app menu for both sports and other apps (other apps include satellite messaging, voice commands, voice calling, Music etc.).

From here, you can pin your favorite sports to the top, as well as sift through your favorites (or find ones you want to do):

Within this realm, you’ve got literal boatloads of sports you can do. Here are the sport modes seen on the Athlete and Adventurer models. Other models may have slightly additional sport modes. For example, the Diver model has an additional ‘Gauge’ diving profile. And the Aviator would have flying modes; the Commander has some additional tactical apps/modes, etc.

Again, here’s the starting point that all units have:

Run, Track Run, Treadmill, Virtual Run, Indoor Track, Walk Indoor, Trail Run, Ultra Run, Hike, Walk, Adventure Race, Bike, Road Bike, Bike Indoor, MTB, eBike, eMTB, Cyclocross, Gravel Bike, Bike Commute, Bike Tour, BMX, Strength, Rucking, Golf, Mountaineering, Bouldering, Fish, Hunt, Disc Golf, Horseback, Expedition, ArcheryX, Obstacle Racing, Inline Skating, Pool Swim, Open Water, Triathlon, Mixed Session, Swimrun, Cardio, Mobility, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Treadmill, Elliptical, Stair Stepper, Row Indoor, XC Ski Indoor, Climb Indoor, Bouldering, Floor Climb, Boxing, Mixed Martial Arts, Jump Rope, Cow Tipping, Scuba Dive, Apnea Dive, Snorkel, Ski, Snowboard, Backcountry Ski, Backcountry Snowboard, XC Classic Ski, XC Skate Ski, Snowshoe, Ice Skating, Snowmobile, SUP, Kayak, Row, Surf, Kiteboarding, Windsurf, Snorkel, Whitewater, Boat, Sail, Sail Race, Sail Expedition, Wakeboard, Wakesurf, Water Ski, Tube, Soccer/Football, American Football, Basketball, Baseball, Softball, Volleyball, Cricket, Lacrosse, Rugby, Field Hockey, Ice Hockey, Ultimate Disc, Gaming, Tennis, Pickleball, Padel, Racquetball, Squash, Badminton, Table Tennis, Platform Tennis, ATV, Snowmobile, Overland, Motocross, Motorcycle, Meditation, Breathwork, Jumpmaster, Track Me, Tempo Training (Golf)

Once you’ve selected a sport mode, you’ll see a pending screen that’ll get GPS satellite lock (assuming outside), as well as heart rate lock. Further, if you’ve got accessory/sensors paired, it’ll go off and find those.

It’s in the settings here that you can do structured workouts, load up a course to navigate, as well as change any number of data fields and settings. Each sport mode has its own data pages you can configure, with your own data field customization.

Now, I will briefly note one of the MARQ Gen3 unique features is the ability to do an ‘Address Search’ on-device. The existing Fenix 9 series allows you to look up points of interest (e.g., a landmark, restaurant, etc.) and navigate to them. But here you can actually type a street address in:

And then with that, you’ll see the other MARQ-unique feature, which is the ability to use predictive text completion (seen at the top):

After you’ve entered in an address, you can navigate to it. Of course, most people are probably gonna load a route instead, or use the map to find a spot, or so on. All of which work exactly the same as past units. With the MARQ Gen3, you’ll get the faster map rendering (including panning and zooming) that came with the new faster processor on the Fenix 9 Pro series.

Ok, with all that sorted, off you go to start navigating and doing your activity.

One of those features is ClimbPro, which will automatically show climb data as you start ascending. However, with the MARQ Gen3, a big-ticket new feature coming is the ability to get ClimbPro details without having a course loaded. Up till now, every past Garmin wearable has required a course to be loaded in order to see the climb details. But now, that’ll happen automatically, like it occurs today on Garmin’s Edge devices (for cycling). But having it for both cycling and hiking/running/walking on the watch will be a super handy change for those of us who don’t always bother to create a course for things.

In any case, I had no issues in terms of daily usage during workouts. This included road bike and gravel bike rides, trail runs, track run workouts, road runs, some gym workouts, indoor trainer rides, as well as the boating and dive activities I’ll get into later.

At the end of a workout, you’ll see all your stats consolidated into some summary pages:

And then likewise, all of this is available in Garmin Connect too.

You’ll also get all of your Training Load & Recovery metrics, by way of Acute Load (for Training Load), as well as the umbrella Garmin Training Readiness feature. Training Readiness looks at not just your Training Load, but also your sleep, heart rate variability, stress, and more.

And just to be clear, buying a $3,000 watch does not exempt you from the right of passage that is Unproductive. Fear not, I successfully unlocked that for a day:

Ultimately, when it comes to all of the sports features here, they remain top of the line within not just the Garmin lineup, but also the industry. I’m super eager to try out the real-time ClimbPro features once those hit. Stay tuned for that down the road (hopefully not far down said road).

LTE & Satellite Connectivity:

The Garmin MARQ Gen3 includes LTE & Satellite messaging connectivity on all models, unless bought in a handful of countries where such connectivity is legally restricted. In those countries, there is a version without LTE & Satellite connectivity.

From a Garmin standpoint, both of these features are more about keeping in touch with close friends and family, rather than your boat repair guy calling you on WhatsApp. Meaning that for LTE for example, it doesn’t share your existing phone number, nor do you even get a phone number for people to call. Instead, calling routes through the Garmin Messenger app, which your friends/family must have. Likewise for satellite messaging, which is even more limited.

Still, I find the LTE functionality mostly just useful for LiveTracking purposes (it’ll automatically start a LiveTrack session and send my friends/family a link). My wife uses it on her Fenix 9 when she’s out running long at night by herself (she hates running with a phone).

The features are divided into two sections, LTE and satellite. When it comes to LTE features, Garmin offers the following features over their LTE network, via LTE-M (which requires lower power as an ecosystem, including voice calling over LTE-M):

– LTE Live two-way voice calls
– LTE LiveTrack (30-second sampling rate)
– LTE Voice Messaging
– LTE Text Messaging
– LTE Weather
– LTE & Satellite Emergency SOS
– LTE Location Check-Ins
– LTE Incident Detection & Assistance

In addition, they also offer satellite text messaging; more on that in a second. Notably, the watches are cross-region compatible due to LTE-M. Meaning, you can use your European model in the US for LTE-M (and satellite), and vice-versa.

Next, for the satellite features, these are more focused on updating status and asking for emergency assistance. Unlike LTE, which just works in the background, all of these features require holding a watch out in front of you to maintain a specific orientation towards a satellite (this is the same with Apple, Google, and others).

– Satellite Messaging (basic texting)
– Satellite position/location check-ins
– Satellite Emergency SOS (via Garmin Response)
– Satellite updating of weather (new in the Fenix 9 Pro)

And then finally, when it comes to the launch of the Fenix 9, Garmin also added a few more things at the same time that are largely tied into the Garmin Messenger app. These aren’t actually dependent on the Fenix 9, but I figured I’d mention it here:

– Added new Garmin Locate feature within Garmin Messenger app
– Added ability to see athlete heart rate, pace, distance, elevation information in Garmin Messenger App

Ok, so with that covered, note that none of these LTE or inReach pieces are free long-term, despite all of their competitors offering the satellite pieces for free. Getting things set up requires setting up an account within Garmin’s inReach platform. This gives you 30 days free, after which it is $9.99/month for unlimited LTE stuffs, and emergency-only Satellite bits. Beyond that, there are additional fees for satellite check-ins/texts that I’ll cover below (or, a higher-priced plan).

From there, you’ll see a menu option on your watch that shows the different connectivity status options, in terms of how and when it leverages both LTE & satellite. Essentially, you can leave it on Auto, force it off/on, and any number of combinations within that.

One of the things I’ve learned over the past year is that this is pretty handy if you actually don’t care about LTE connectivity; it’s best to just set it to ‘Satellite Only’, which means to essentially shut off LTE on the watch entirely, and just use my phone connection. Since the Satellite messaging pieces require a bunch of knowingly manual steps, it’s not something that can happen in the background anyway.

I dive into all the nuances of the LTE & Satellite features in both my Fenix 8 Pro & Fenix 9 Reviews (with a sprawling LTE & Satellite section). This includes voice calling, transcription of voice messages automatically, and plenty more.

That said, in terms of satellite messaging, which requires no cellular service nearby, probably one of the most notable things you’ll need to do first is to pair it up to the Garmin Messenger app on your phone. You don’t need this app again once you’ve done this once. But if you don’t, then all your Messenger contacts won’t sync to the watch. Sure, Emergency SOS will work just fine, but otherwise you won’t be able to send messages to friends/family. Honestly, this just seems super clunky to me. I totally understand all the Garmin technical reasons behind the scenes for this, but I simply don’t care Garmin, figure it out. It shouldn’t be this clunky for any user.

In any case, with that said, note that currently satellite messaging coverage is essentially limited to Europe and North America. And within that, not quite all regions. Here’s a map of it:

Assuming you’re within coverage range, you can open up the Messenger app on your watch, which allows you to select pre-canned messages (both Garmin ones, and ones you can customize), as well as simply type a message out. Likewise, you can also use the Garmin Messenger app on your phone (connected via Bluetooth) to type out messages much faster.

Once that’s done, you’ll choose to send. For this you’ll stick your arm out in front of you, and it’ll give you instructions on orienting your body and wrist accordingly. In my testing with the MARQ Gen3 models, all messages sent within 30 seconds, even including through some light tree branches.

Lastly, as you’d expect, there are the Garmin SOS features, leveraging Garmin’s Response Center, for emergencies. You can access that via the controls menu, which then gives you 10 seconds to cancel it, in case it was accidentally activated. As with the other features, it’ll first try via LTE, then satellite.

Ultimately, I find the Garmin satellite feature handy on Garmin watches. Sure, my phone already has some sort of satellite messaging capability, but I might not always have my phone. And in my case I live barely 2-3 minutes out my front door into no-cellular areas of empty wilderness. Further, as many divers have pointed out, having a way to reach a dive boat after you surface can be handy, especially for drift dives, if the party has broken up a bit. And knowing that’ll work even without cellular can be clutch.

Scuba Diving & Boating:

Now in my case, I had both a Diver unit and an Adventurer unit. Practically speaking, all units support scuba diving & free diving, just like the Fenix 9 units (and since the Fenix 8 units). However, the Diver also has additional integration with Garmin marine systems that the Fenix doesn’t have (but the Fenix cousin, the Quatix series, does have).

The Diver also has a few extra diving features that the Fenix 9 doesn’t have. They are:

– Full Coverage preloaded DiveView Maps
– Dive Readiness Feature
– NDL Aware Feature
– Gauge Mode

The DiveView maps in particular show you depth (both for diving as well as boating), and then also show you nearby dive sites.

So, let’s briefly run through the dive features first. As a brief aside, while digging into a few things, I stumbled upon Garmin’s Dive features technical explainer site, which is surprisingly comprehensive in terms of explaining all their features and the specific science behind it. Note that not all features are on the MARQ Gen3 (for example, features tied to air integration). But if you’re into dive geekery, I thought it was kinda neat.

Anyway, for this post I’ll focus on scuba, simply because that’s what I did the last few weeks (I’ve got some free-diving coming back up again in a few weeks). To start you’ll select a Dive type (e.g., Scuba), and then open it up. One of the options you have though is for it to automatically engage the moment you go 1.5m deep in the water. In any case, by opening it up first, you’ll get your GPS lock, which is then recorded as the entry/exit points in your dive log.

Here you can customize any settings you want about the dive. This includes water type, tank settings, conservatism preferences, etc… Further, you can change your data field configurations to show specific metrics you want to see (or don’t want to see). Again, the MARQ Gen3 doesn’t support air tank integration like their Descent units. I do feel like for the Diver model specifically, this is a bit of an odd omission. I get from a technical conformity standpoint that would have likely opened up an entire manufacturing can of worms for Garmin, but isn’t that the point of a $3,000 watch called ‘Diver’? That’s precisely when that can should be opened up.

In any case, with all that sorted out, off into the water you go. The moment you get down into the water, it’ll start tracking the dive. You’ll see your metrics automatically.  One of these days I’ll get good at taking underwater shots of watches. Today was not that day.

As with Garmin’s other dive-certified units, I had no issues with it automatically tracking my dive metrics throughout my dives. It works exactly in-line with a Fenix 9 Pro and Apple Watch Ultra 4 I had on all my dives. All of which are fully certified depth gauge dive computers down to 40m. Remember that’s the certification level of the depth gauge, the actual watch, from a case standpoint, is certified down to 100m.

Once I started to surface, it’ll automatically notify me of my safety stop, and track that. Further, if I ascended too fast at some point, it’ll also have notified me of that too.

After I reach the surface, it’ll start a countdown timer to end the dive automatically. Assuming you raise your wrist above the water, it’ll also track the exit point (via GPS). This is then saved within the dive log.

These logs are accessible via the Garmin Dive app, which pulls from your Garmin Connect account. You can update additional dive log details here, as well as add photos/etc…

In the case of the Garmin MARQ Diver, it actually has a few extra features the Fenix 9 doesn’t have, such as Diver Readiness. This is essentially like Garmin’s Training Readiness, except it also looks at your historical dive data, to see whether or not you dive frequently enough that your body can adapt to the dives quickly. Further, it gives you warnings not to do hard workouts afterwards (just like you also get No-Fly warnings like on the Fenix).

Additionally, when it comes to planning a dive, the extra and included depth maps will show you depth, but also show you dive sites.

You can view this by using the Dive Planner option, which lets you lookup nearby Dive Sites:

Meanwhile, on the boating side, I’ve been using it a bit there, though none of the boats I have access to have Garmin marine equipment on them, so I couldn’t use the autopilot/connected features. If someone would like do donate a fancier boat to me, I’d be happy to ensure compliance.

Instead, I mostly used it from the standpoint of course/speed/etc, as well as checking depth using the marine maps that show depth information:

Note that I did have an odd quirk where, when in a boating profile, the land-based TopoGraphic maps aren’t enumerating correctly. In this case I see the marine maps for the watery portions, but the land portions aren’t properly showing anything except blackness. In talking to Garmin, this is already fixed in a firmware update that’ll likely land in my device in the coming days.

In any case, I do feel like it’s worth mentioning one other quirk, which is around the anchor alarm feature. Perhaps it’s just me being new to Garmin’s implementation of this feature, but frankly, it doesn’t make much sense the way it’s implemented. For those not familiar with boating, an anchor alarm is essentially a GPS-based geofence that you enable so that if your anchor drags and you start drifting, then it’ll sound a loud/annoying alarm to let you know. You can set it on Garmin Quatix watches, Fenix watches, and probably some others.

However, where this kinda falls apart is that you have to end your current boating activity entirely. You can’t merely pause it, or ‘Resume later’. Thus, if you’ve sailed somewhere where you want to anchor for a bit (perhaps a couple hours) before continuing on, you can’t set the anchor alarm without ending that activity. In the hiking world, that’d be akin to being forced to end your hike merely cause you wanted to pause for a few minutes to have lunch.

Now some might argue that you’d normally use this feature when anchoring for the day, going into night. Except that ignores the marine reality here: If you’re anchoring for the night, it’s extremely likely your boat already has an anchor alarm feature built into it. Whereas, inversely, if you’re boat lacks cabins (more of a day craft), then it’s more likely you don’t have an anchor alarm built into it, and thus the benefit of the watch feature.

In my case, the boats I go out with are more for day-use. I just want to ensure when I’m on anchor that I’m not dragging anchor into the rocks. This weekend was a great example of that with a bit of swell, but trying to anchor as close as possible to the shore, to minimize that swell.

Anyway, I know this is a first-world problem, and it seems like one that’s been around a long time. I just can’t decide whether nobody bothers to use the feature, or just shrugs and assumes it’s always this way. Or maybe Garmin Marine products just need more ‘me’ in their life reviewing them to point out these weird issues.

Nonetheless, setting all that aside, I had no issues with the marine or scuba feature I did use.

GPS & Heart Rate Accuracy:

The MARQ Gen3 shares the same Garmin ELEVATE Gen5 optical heart rate sensor as numerous other watches before it, including the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro series. Further, it shares the same GPS components and antenna design as the Fenix 9 Series. Though Garmin did note that they used different nano-molding technology to deal with the layers associated with the antenna design and case on the MARQ series, allowing them to achieve a thinner design than normal bonding found on the Fenix 9.

Nonetheless, I still checked the accuracy of the heart rate and GPS systems across numerous workouts, both inside and outside, and across different sport modes. So, let’s just run through some of those.

First up, we’ve got an interval workout from a few days ago:

As you can see, it’s basically spot-on with the chest strap, so kudos there.

Looking at the GPS track for that, the area was relatively easy, but it was also loop after loop after loop, so any inconsistencies would be easy to see.

Specifically on the turns, where here it nailed each one exactly where I was each time (on the deserted road). The COROS Pace 4 Pro was slightly offset.

After that, I’ve got a trail run I did. Starting off on the heart rate side of things, things look good here, except for one brief spike, which I believe it tied to a short/steep downhill section. Basically, classic cadence lock where the heart rate locks onto your running cadence/footsteps. This is mildly interesting to me, because I run this steep hill at least once a week, and this is the first time I’ve seen Garmin’s Gen5 optical HR sensor trip up on it.

In any case, looking at the GPS side of things, from a wider standpoint, things look pretty solid:

Looking at a section in a ravine with trees, no issues. All the units are all reasonably close, within a few meters of each other:

And likewise, later along some cliffs coming back up a trail, no issues. As with the rest of the run.

I did, however, see both the Garmin Fenix 9 & MARQ Gen3 struggle a bit from a barometric altimeter standpoint here. That section where they split apart from the Apple Watch & COROS unit isn’t correct. I was standing there on a cliff edge taking photos, and you can start to see the Garmin units separate. I don’t know whether that’s a barometric altimeter issue or a terrain-locking issue (perhaps thinking I was off the cliff). Either way, it’s the first time I’ve seen it on any Garmin unit in many years.

Now let’s look at an outdoor run I just did last night. Nothing crazy, but nice and sustained through some high building areas. First, looking at the heart rate, we can see nothing of note there (I used a silicone band here):

And then on the GPS side, at a side level, nothing of note here:

Looking at some tall building areas with taller hotels, as well as under a building with a swimming pool above me (for real, it’s like half a football field long), the MARQ handles well there. Though, it is slightly in the buildings a few meters at a different point earlier for a few seconds. This was with the default GPS settings (which is SatIQ).

Ultimately, I’m seeing performance here that matches the Garmin Fenix 9 series, which is industry-leading in terms of GPS accuracy as well as elevation accuracy. And then further, from a heart rate standpoint, I also see similar performance to that, which tends to be among the best in the industry as well.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Garmin MARQ Odds & Ends:

I don’t know where to put these things, but I went to a media presentation about the watch, and I thought these tidbits were interesting, and likely wouldn’t otherwise see the light of day within the general fancy-watch media crowd. Not because they aren’t covering things in detail, but just because I suspect they’re focused on other areas. Anyways, in no particular order:

-Uploads per year: There are “approximately 6 million MARQ workout/activity uploads per year” currently to Garmin Connect (from Gen1/Gen2), as part of the far larger “billions” of workout/activity uploads each year to Garmin Connect from all Garmin users

– Fenix 1 Users: There are still some 4,000 active Fenix 1 users uploading to Garmin Connect daily. While this isn’t MARQ, Garmin’s point is that people do indeed use these watches for upwards of a decade. There’s nothing wrong with it in a few years, aside from consumerism driving you to buy a new model.

– Increase in retailers: They’ve had a 4x increase in MARQ retailers since MARQ Gen 2 launched. Note that there is a huge slate of requirements to be a MARQ retailer, just like any other luxury watch brand would have. For example, you generally won’t find MARQ watches on Amazon. Though sometimes they find their way through random distribution or small resale quirks.

– Increase in sales: They say they’ve had “8x the amount of sales turnover” since MARQ Gen2. Meaning, there’s clearly demand for this product. Given we’re on the 4th generation of it now (assuming you include Chronos as the first generation), Garmin wouldn’t be sticking around if it wasn’t making them money. Garmin has very clear internal rules around financial ROI/margins.

– Driving new Garmin customers: They noted that 50% of MARQ customers are new to Garmin in terms of wearable or sports products (they might have boat or aviation gear, however, in their cockpits).

– The Lack of Metal Bands: You’ll notice there are no metal bands for MARQ Gen 3, just like there are no metal bands for the Fenix 9 Pro series. This is due to the LTE & Satellite antenna communication components in the current design. It sounds like their long-term hope is to be able to engineer some solution in future hardware. This should have no meaningful impact on GPS accuracy or other features.

– The most popular MARQ activities. When it comes to existing owners and what they’re uploading to Garmin Connect, here’s the current breakdown:

That’s it, I’m out of interesting tidbits at this point from the media briefings that I didn’t already include elsewhere.

Wrap-Up:

Writing a review for a watch like this is tricky. There’s a simple reality that for a large portion of the population, this watch will seem like a waste of money. But the same could and would be spent on photography gear, I and many other photographers buy. A $2,000 lens on a $2,000 camera body, and that’s just one lens (a lens that I managed to flood the other day, costing me another $1,000 in repairs…sigh). Sure, that gear will last many years, but as Garmin pointed out with their Fenix 1 metrics above, people can and do still use these watches long term (more than a decade in that case).

And now finally with the MARQ Gen 3 units, Garmin has a watch that doesn’t lag (far) behind their premium Fenix watches. Instead, the opposite – it’s finally a watch that tops the Garmin lineup with all the features of a Fenix and then a slate of additional hardware and software features. Whether or not it’s worth the price Garmin sets is somewhat of an aside; it’s that there’s finally not a caveat on it being a subpar watch feature/spec-wise but with fancy materials. Now, it’s both.

In terms of my usage, overall I had very few bugs over the last near-month with it. And all the items I did identify (mainly around mapping) are slated to be fixed in a firmware update in the near term. Of course, Garmin hasn’t yet released the real-time ClimbPro features, so those will have to wait to see how they shake out. You can of course still use the existing course-based ClimbPro as I did, without issues.

As for whether or not I’d buy one? If I were to buy one, I’m almost certain it’d be the Adventurer, despite the slightly added features of the Diver. But those features aren’t really make-or-break for me. But at the same time, with me testing watches as my job, this just wouldn’t get as much use as it would for someone who puts it on their wrist 24×7. Therefore, it’s hard for me to justify spending the money (especially with all the other toys on my list to buy). But unlike in the past, at least I could see the path to a case in front of the accountant (my wife). Albeit, it’d still probably get rejected – but at least not because she doesn’t find them good-looking. She does. Which, is a pretty big step in getting something approved.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Fitbit Edge Announced: Everything You Need to Know!
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

Fitbit has decided there will be no Fitbit Charge 7. Instead, the device will now be known as the Fitbit Edge, and with that, it follows more closely in line with the user interface of the Google Pixel Watch 5, alongside technology stashed inside the recent screenless Fitbit Air. If there were any questions as to whether or not Google remains committed to the Fitbit branding (in name), this would certainly answer that. Fitbit as a brand is clearly here to stay, even if they renamed the app to Google Health earlier this year.

The Fitbit Edge is a small-screen activity tracker, just like the Fitbit Charge series before it. With it, Google has made some big changes, mostly good, but not all good. On the ‘good’ side, they’re claiming the GPS is now actually functional. Previously, on the Fitbit Charge 5 & Charge 6, the GPS only worked if you loosened the band substantially, but when you did that, heart rate stopped working. For real. They even admitted it was a design choice at the time. Now, Fitbit is saying GPS should be “40% better” than the Charge 6. Plus, they added an altimeter, for both stair tracking and elevation tracking.

Beyond that, the Fitbit Edge gets all of the automatic workout recognition pieces of the Fitbit Air, except as of today, that sport list goes from like 10 sports to roughly 100 sports. Meaning even if you don’t press any buttons, it’ll still figure out that you’re pole dancing. Or…maybe that icon is a stand-up paddleboarder. It’s fuzzy. Atop that, the user interface now matches the Pixel Watch 5, which is cleaned up. Oh, and it’s got a ‘real’ button now, versus a touchable pseudo-button. But there are some downsides too – like no more Google Pay (contactless payments). And the price has significantly increased, up to $179USD from the usual $99-$129 that the Charge 6 floats at these days.

In any case, I’ve got a unit that I can start sharing hands-on details on tomorrow, but for now, here’s everything you need to know.

What’s New vs Charge 6:

The Fitbit Edge is the next version of the Fitbit Charge 6, which came out in 2023. Here’s how it’s different:

– Increased screen/display by 46% (has 1.34” display)
– Case thickness is 11.5mm
– Added physical side button that actually clicks (previous was just a touch area)
– Added altimeter (for stair tracking, as well as elevation tracking)
– Added automatic workout detection (now supports 100 sports)
– Increased supported manual workout profiles to 50 workout profiles
– Made user-replaceable/serviceable battery (the first Fitbit-branded product to do so)
– GPS accuracy improvement claimed at 40% more accurate (via new GPS chipset, and new aluminum case design)
– Switched to a more modern user interface, matching the Pixel Watch 5 series
– Added structured workout support
– Added support for dual usage with Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air (e.g., switching back and forth seamlessly)
– Added fast charging (5 minutes gets you 1 day of usage)
– Removed Google Pay (NFC Contactless payments)
– Removed EDA Scan feature (but does have continuous stress monitoring in the background)
– Changed the band attachment mechanism (old Fitbit habits die hard)
– Switched the charger to the same charger as the Fitbit Air (hey, at least they picked something else they already had this time)
– Added a bunch of band accessory types
– Price increased to $179 (officially the Charge 6 was $159 previously, but realistically it sat between $99 and $129 virtually all the time)
– Also a Stephen Curry model at $219 (US, Canada, EMEA)
– Pre-orders start today; availability October 27th.

In terms of some other general specs, just for recap purposes:

– Same claimed 7-day battery life
– Still has heart rate broadcasting feature via Bluetooth (though it can be a bit funky in terms of compatibility)
– Still has music control of your phone’s music (no onboard music storage)
– Still has Google Maps turn-by-turn directions (with phone)
– Still has smartphone notifications (more integration on Android than iOS)
– Still has full sleep tracking
– Still has continuous heart rate monitoring (background and workout)
– Still supports high & low heart rate alerts
– Supports the Google Health Guardian features announced a few months ago
– You can do quick replies on Android, though not on iOS devices
– Has FDA/EU approved medical ECG functionality, including background Afib detection
– Includes skin temperature sensor
– Supports Steps, Distance, Active Zone Minutes, VO2Max, Floor/elevation, Cardio Load, and many more metrics
– Two sizes of bands (see specs below)
– Water resistance level is 5ATM, and IP68 for dust protection

Finally, for lack of anywhere else to stick it, Google also announced a multi-year partnership with Flo Health (which has 80 million users), which will allow bidirectional syncing of data between the two platforms starting early next year. From Flo Health to Google Health, you’ll be able to pull your cycle data in. And then from Google Health to Flo Health, you’ll be able to send resting heart rate, skin temperature, heart rate variability, and sleep metrics. Further, on the Google Health side, it’ll leverage your cycle-tracking information for both general suggestions as well as workout suggestions. Finally, Google also noted:

“We will partner to build new products that are specifically designed for women, with a deep integration of Flo’s women’s health insights and algorithms with our expertise in wearable hardware and advanced sensors.”

It’ll be interesting to see if that’s hardware products or software “products”. Further, they noted there are upcoming plans around dedicated women’s health research initiatives (I assume that means large-scale studies you could opt-in to). Note that in the case of the Flo Health integration, Google says this is all optional, of course, and you can enable and then subsequently turn on/off things as you see fit.

Again, I’ll have much more hands-on details coming, starting tomorrow, but for now, let’s get to all the model options.

Detailed Tech & Model Specs:

The Fitbit Air case comes in 5 different colorways, and then with that there are approximately 2,328 band options. Starting off with the core options you can buy, they are as follows:

– Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band
– Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band
– Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Stephen Curry Special Edition

And here’s a look at each of these. First, the Matte Black model with black band:

Then the Polished silver model with fog band:

Then the Satin Pyrite Aluminum case model with olive band:

Next, the Champagne Gold case with canyon band:

Oh, and there are the metal link bands too:

Finally, looking at the tech specs, here’s a whole slate of things that may or may not be interesting to you:

– Display is 1.34”/34mm AMOLED display, supporting an always-on configuration
– Display supports adjustable brightness
– Bluetooth 5.4
– Processor: Ambiq AP5 MCU
– GPS chipset supports GPS+Galileo in US, and GPS+Galileo+GLONASS+BeiDou+QZSS outside of US
– Onboard memory: 64MB NOR flash memory, 7 days of detailed motion data (minute intervals), 30 days of daily totals, heart rate at 2-second intervals
– Internal sensors: Altimeter, Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2), Multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, Photoplethysmography (PPG) optical heart rate sensor, Ambient light sensor, Far-field skin temperature sensor
– Battery is 65mAh
– Fully end-user replaceable battery
– Charging speed: 5 minutes of fast charging for 1 day of battery life, or 100% in 90 minutes
– Requires iOS 16.4 or newer, and Android 11 or newer
– Fitbit Edge Weight: 17.7g without band
– Fitbit Edge Dimensions: 39.22 x 25.56 mm
– Fitbit Edge Height/Thickness: 11.58mm
– Case is made from 100% recycled aluminum
– Active band: Silicone with “soft-touch coating”
– Active Band Sizing: Small fits wrists 130-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band: “Recycled polyester yarns with water-repellent coating and stainless steel lugs, as well as a raised interior print for increased airflow.”
– Stephen Curry band sizing (US): Small fits wrists 135-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band sizing (EU/Canada): Single-size fits wrists 150-195mm around
– Water resistance: 5ATM/50 meters
– Dust immersion resistance: IP68

On the manual workout profile side, here are the workout profiles that are supported on the Fitbit Edge. Note these are a subset of the automatic detection list, which is around 100 activities.

I definitely appreciate having all of these profiles available on-device, rather than just a very basic set. Which I suppose is the general trend in watches/wearables the last year or two: More workout profile options is better.

Next, when it comes to automatic workout types, here’s how those are broken out:

Core sports without any context:

I do want to point out that I’d love to have been a fly on the wall in conference rooms at Google when they debated putting the ‘Hoeing’ activity type in there. I just can’t wait for the Instagram meme jokes that come from that.

(As a geeky aside, it’s astonishing how detailed/comprehensive Google/Fitbit has become with their technical information, imagery, videos, and detailed documents explaining things. While I get full briefings, devices sent on time, and seemingly 24×7 responses within minutes, even on holiday weekends, it’s just such a difference to what some companies do, where every question is almost begging for answers. When companies make it easy to cover your products, you’ll find media tend to cover it with more details.)

Some Fitbit Air Updates:

As part of all of this, the Fitbit Air gets a few quite notable updates. First and the biggest is a massive expansion of the automatic workout detection profiles, from roughly 10 (though realistically it was less than that), to 100 sport profiles. I don’t yet have an official text listing of those profiles, though here is a nifty screenshot of all the icons that are included in this listing:

At present, I can only assume that the one with the person holding onto the pole is pole dancing. Sure, some might argue SUP. But what’s the fun in that? I’ll update this once I have a full listing. [Update: Just added in full list above. No pole dancing…but hey, there’s ‘Hoeing’.]

Do note that Fitbit says some of this is coming from understanding your patterns, rather than straight sport recognition. When it comes to automatic workout detection, there’s sorta two levels. The first is the device/platform (most processing is done in the cloud) actually being able to figure out that you were running, or cycling, or mountain biking. That’s the most ideal scenario. The second level is when a platform knows that you did something, but is a bit fuzzy on what exactly. In those cases, they can look at your history and context and say “Oh, every Saturday morning she goes mountain biking and she updated past activities to specify that, so this must be mountain biking because it’s Saturday morning”. That’s so-so in my opinion, because it’s better than nothing, but still not really nailing the movement recognition as good as Whoop does.

Nonetheless, Fitbit says that with this new algorithm they are “2x more accurate” in detections, and reduced “missed workouts by more than half”. Workouts must still meet the minimum 15-minute threshold as in the past.

Next, there are some new Metal Mesh bands coming out for the Fitbit Air. This includes a Champagne Gold or Polished Silver band for $69, or you can buy the Champagne Gold band with a Fitbit Air for $149 (so basically a $20 savings). Here’s what that looks like:

And here’s the polished silver one:

And finally, as previously announced, the Health Guardian feature will start unlocking reports later this month for existing Fitbit Air users, as well as other Fitbit users.

Once the firmware rolls out for the Fitbit Air and the new sport profiles, I’ll start digging into it and report back.

Going Forward:

Now, starting tomorrow, I can start sharing details from the device itself. Of course, having such lineage to both the Fitbit Charge 6 and their more recent products like the Fitbit Air & Pixel Watch 5, I don’t really expect any sort of crazy surprises here. However, the sport mode expansions are real and quite legit. Up to 100 sports now in auto-detect mode for both Fitbit Air & Fitbit Edge is a huge shift, and now much more competitive with Whoop (at least in theory; we’ll have to see in reality).

While the unit is priced higher, I think some of the added features may make it worthwhile. Notably, the structured workouts support, added altimeter for stairs/elevation, the theoretical improvements in GPS accuracy, plus the bigger display. Of course, the removal of Google Wallet/Pay seems like an odd choice to me. In this scenario, especially for iPhone users, it’s not really pushing those users up to the Google Pixel Watch, because that doesn’t work for iOS (just Android). Perhaps eventually Google will unlock the Pixel Watch for iOS users too.

In any case, plenty more to come shortly on the Fitbit Edge as I dive into testing.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: Garmin Enduro 4 Everything You Need To Know: What’s Actually New?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

Garmin has announced the new Enduro 4, which takes the existing Enduro 3 and Fenix 9-ifies it. This follows the same pattern that Garmin did when it announced the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series back a few years ago. This means that the Enduro 4 gets some updated hardware internals, such as a faster processor and more RAM, as well as doubled storage for more offline maps. With those more powerful internals, you’re getting faster mapping features. Plus of course, the Enduro 4 gets all the Fenix 9 software features (which Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 users are also getting).

There are also some slight material changes too, mainly with the band and bezel. They’ve swapped out the UltraFit band for the new ComfortFit ones, which is a great change in my opinion. I’ve been using the new ComfortFit ones with the Fenix 9 series, and they’re awesome. Further, they changed up the color of the bezel, which you may or may not like depending on your personal color palette preferences.

In any case, I’ve started to put the Enduro 4 through its paces, though given all the other wearables slated for the next 6 days, wrist space is very limited right now. So for the moment, let’s just get into how things are different.

What’s New:

The Enduro 3 to Enduro 4 upgrade of hardware may not seem like a big one, mostly because you have to remember the whole point of the Enduro series is to *minimize* things that burn lots of battery. Meaning, adding in battery-hungry features like LTE & inReach (satellite messaging) are sorta the last thing you want Garmin to do.

However, more critical here is Garmin’s decision to bring virtually all the new Fenix 9 features back to the Fenix 8/8 Pro & Enduro 3 watches. Thus, by definition, with them all being treated as a single software platform, it becomes a more minor hardware update (akin to what Apple does each year). The point isn’t really for Enduro 3 owners to buy up (because you’re getting all the cool new Fenix 9 software features for free), but rather, for Enduro 1 & Enduro 2 folks to buy up. Make sense?

In any case, here’s what’s new hardware-wise:

– Faster processor for maps (specifically the Fenix 9 base processor, not the Fenix 9 Pro processor)
– 50% more RAM for map speed increases
– Doubled storage from 32GB to 64GB
– Went from black titanium bezel to a grey titanium bezel
– Cleaned up bezel to have fewer green/yellow markings
– Changed the GPS mode names to match Fenix 9, though the battery life remains identical
– Changed from UltraFit band to ComfortFit with QuickFit (trust me, it’s far better)
– New band increased total unit weight by 3g, case weight is identical (total weight from 63g to 66g)
– Same $899 price as the Enduro 3 (though the Enduro 3 went on sale this week to $799 with a bunch of other Garmin things for Amazon Prime Days)

Here you can see the new band/clasp system as part of the ComfortFit bands:

Meanwhile, here are the things that stay the same from Enduro 3 to Enduro 4:

– Same exact 1.4” MIP display panel at 280x280px
– Same exact Solar components
– Same exact smartwatch battery life (36 days smartwatch, 90 days with Solar)
– Same rough GPS battery life (see chart), though with new mode names
– Same thickness and case size (51mm)

Here’s the battery ‘chart’ showing all the battery modes/times:

Enduro 4 Battery Specs/Claims:
Smartwatch: Up to 36 days/90 days with solar*
Low Power Watch Mode: Up to 92 days/unlimited with solar*
Activity Mode (Normal): Up to 80 hours/144 hours with solar**
Activity Mode + Music (Normal): Up to 22 hours/25 hours with solar**
Activity Mode (Max Battery): Up to 210 hours/unlimited with solar**
Activity Mode (Extended Battery): Up to 120 hours/320 hours with solar**
Activity Mode (Max Accuracy): Up to 60 hours/90 hours with solar**
Expedition Mode: Up to 77 days/unlimited with solar*

*Solar charging, assuming all-day wear with 3 hours per day outside in 50,000 lux conditions
**Solar charging, assuming use in 50,000 lux conditions; assuming typical use with SatIQ technology

Here’s a side-by-side photo of the two units out tanning in the direct sun.

(At left, Enduro 3, at right Enduro 4)

Then, from a software standpoint, here are all the new features. All but the last few features are coming to the Enduro 3 via software update (in fact, some, like the Ski Erg features, already did last week). However, this just gets you all of them right now. The last few ones are dependent on the new mapping engine, which in turn requires the faster processor/more RAM:

– Added new Garmin Epic features, which group multi-day events/adventures (both on-device, and on Garmin Connect)
– New Stamina zone concept
– Added New Stamina Endurance time concept
– Added New Stamina trending feature (on Garmin Connect)
– Added New Running & Cycling Stamina graphs/curves
– Added New Rucking/Pack-Weight calorie breakout for activities (in multiple sport profiles)
– Revamped algorithms around pack-weight to more accurately cover calorie impacts
– Added New Rucking target calculator on-watch: Can tell you how far you need to go for a certain goal & pack weight
– Added ability to change pack-weight mid-activity
– Added Dedicated Rucking Reports (summarizing pack weight, calories, elevation, pace)
– Added Rucking Multisport mode option
– Added New on-device Rucking structured workouts with GoRuck
– Added New Ski Erg Profile (officially called ‘XC Ski Indoor’)
– Huge update/change for Indoor Rowing
– Added new heart rate zones for rowing, and max heart rate
– Added new power zones and power curves for running
– Added new indoor rowing FTP values/estimation
– Added new indoor rowing VO2Max values
– Added lactate threshold for rowing, and performance condition
– Added indoor rowing activity profile countdown timer (5-second timer, to let you get ready)
– Added support for indoor rowing to update Training Status (e.g., Productive, Unproductive, etc.)
– Added Rolling GAP as a data field (both kilometer and mile)
– Added Rolling GAP as a structured workout target option
– Added new ‘Field Tools’ feature, including ABC, measure height, reference point, and more

And then, here’s another set of new features that the Enduro 4 & Fenix 9 series get, but the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series won’t get, due to hardware constraints dependent on the increased RAM & processor (or, in the case of the GPS modes, so they don’t have to re-test all of the existing models’ official specs for new battery claims).

– Mapping: New Perspective view (sorta a tilted map view)
– Mapping Performance: Smoother/faster zoom
– Mapping Performance: More responsive heading updates (orientation)
– Added new ArcheryX feature
– Added new Dynamic Battery GPS modes, which basically simplify the naming of the satellite modes

Again, if you have an existing Garmin Enduro 3 or Fenix 8 series watch, you’ll eventually get all of the features in the first list. The timelines on that remain fuzzy, but Garmin says it won’t be this year for everything, though some features have already started showing up in recent updates.

Key Differences to Fenix 9?

(At left, Enduro 3, center Enduro 4, right Fenix 9 Pro Solar 47mm)

Now, real quick, what are the key differences between the Enduro 4 vs Fenix 9? Just like with the Enduro 3 vs Fenix 8 series, this is mostly about the Enduro series being optimized for higher battery life, but also reduced costs. They do away with extra things required for diving, LTE, speakers/mic, etc., and that in turn gives you more battery life and a ‘cheaper Fenix’ in the name of Enduro. Again, remember the Enduro & Fenix watches are under the same software watch family. All software releases for the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series were identical and grouped together, and the same is now true with the Enduro 4 & Fenix 9.

In any case, here are the key differences (when focused specifically on the SOLAR-MIP models):

– Enduro 4 has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar models
– Enduro 4 is far lighter than the Fenix 9 (66g vs 102g for the Fenix 9 Pro Solar 51mm non-inReach)
– Enduro 4 is slightly thinner than the Fenix 9 (15.7mm vs 16.6mm for Fenix 9 Pro Solar 51mm)
– Enduro 4 is offered in one size (51mm), whereas Fenix 9 is offered in three sizes (43/47/51mm, though MIP-Solar only in 47/51mm)
– Fenix 9 series has depth gauge and scuba/freediving features (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 series has induction buttons for better water resistance
– Fenix 9 series has a speaker/microphone (Enduro 4 has a simple beeper, no microphone
– Fenix 9 series has voice control/calling features with that microphone (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 Pro series has a faster processor than the Fenix 9 base/Enduro 4 units
– Fenix 9 Pro series has full Titanium case options (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 Pro series has a green LED flashlight (plus the white/red that Enduro 4 has)
– Fenix 9 Pro inReach models have LTE & inReach Satellite Message (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 base starts at $999 (AMOLED only), Fenix 9 Pro from $1,099 (AMOLED/SOLAR), Fenix 9 Pro inReach/LTE from $1,199 (Enduro 4 is $899)

When it comes to those LTE & inReach Satellite features found on the Fenix 9 Pro inReach models, these are those features (none of which are on Enduro 4):

– LTE Live two-way voice calls
– LTE LiveTrack (30-second sampling rate)
– LTE Voice Messaging
– LTE Text Messaging
– LTE Weather
– LTE & Satellite Emergency SOS
– LTE Location Check-Ins
– LTE Incident Detection & Assistance
– Satellite Messaging (basic texting)
– Satellite position/location check-ins
– Satellite Emergency SOS (via Garmin Response)
– Satellite updating of weather (new in the Fenix 9 Pro)

In terms of some quick-hit similarities between the Enduro 4 and Fenix 9, this is things at a high level:

– Both run the same software and all the same features
– Both have Garmin’s Elevate Gen5 optical HR sensor
– Both have medically certified ECG hardware/features
– Both have Sapphire glass display covers (lens)
– Both have LED flashlights (but again, Fenix 9 Pro models have green LED too)
– Both have onboard offline maps
– Both have onboard storage for offline music (Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, MP3 files, etc.), to play back with Bluetooth headphones
– Both have WiFi syncing support
– Both have full ANT+ & Bluetooth Sensor support

Again, there are a gazillion more things that are the same between those two watches (primarily on the software side), but those are the main things to remember.

Mapping Speed Differences:

Now, with everything essentially being the same software-wise and display/battery-wise, the only real difference between the two is around the increased processing power, increased RAM, and then,  in turn,  the downstream improvements to map processing that Garmin has touted for the Enduro 4 as well as Fenix 9 series units.

Remember that in this case, the Enduro 4 shares the same processor as the base Fenix 9 units, not the slightly faster Fenix 9 Pro series processor. That new base processor is still faster than the Fenix 8 series units (which the Enduro 3 shared), and Garmin says a fair chunk of the improvements to speed is also coming from the rebuilt mapping engine, which requires that 50% improvement in RAM.

In any case, all that said, in terms of the speed improvements I see, like with the Fenix 9, it’s mostly ‘shrug’. Yes, they are faster, but not massively so. Here are some simple tests I did:

Speed test: Open a course file of 50KM/31mi:
Enduro 3: ~8 seconds
Enduro 4: ~8 seconds
Fenix 9 Pro: ~8 seconds

Speed test: Create a running route to a point across the island over a mountain range ( 23KM away as the bird flew, 30KM as the runner went):
Enduro 3: 1min 15sec
Enduro 4: 45sec
Fenix 9 Pro: 28sec

In the video, I also show some differences panning around, for which there is a notable difference, but mainly about 1-2 seconds of extra render time in my mountain-ish area with just light trails/terrain. Perhaps in some city scenario or such, but realistically that’s not where I tend to use the mapping features of any Garmin watch (I have my phone for that).

Now, as I noted in the Fenix 9 review, it’s easy to compare the maps from COROS zooming around/panning around, but the simple reality is those aren’t fully routable maps. They are essentially pictures/tiles that just load, whereas Garmin is actually rendering up a full routable map that you can route on-device to any other point without a phone. Creating a new route on a COROS device requires a phone. On an Amazfit device, you can create on-device routes only for round-trip routes, and even then, they almost always fail (as every reviewer has pointed out). Likewise, Garmin’s maps have far more information depth than anyone else.

Now, don’t mistake me pointing out map facts from me saying you actually need the on-device route generation that Garmin has in everyday life. As I noted in my Fenix 9 review, I can literally count on one hand the number of times in the real world I use the on-device route creation in real life (aside for review funsies purposes) as roughly twice. And neither time was super critical. Handy, yes…critical no.

In just the same way that while I don’t find that feature super useful, neither do I find just randomly panning around the map like a candy-fueled toddler, like every YouTuber likes to do. I simply don’t do that in real life out on multi-day treks, or even long single-day ultras. Do I occasionally check something a few hundred meters away? Sure. Does it take an extra 1-2 seconds on a Garmin? Sure. Am I upset that I have to wait 1-2 seconds longer in the middle of a 17-hour day? Nah. Do I wish Garmin’s maps were faster? Of course.

All of these things can be true. It doesn’t have to be fanboyism.

In any event, one new mapping feature is the new Perspective View, as seen on the Fenix 9. Here’s what that looks like side-by-side with the Enduro 3’s straight-down view:

(At left, Enduro 3, at right Enduro 4)

I’ve grown to like this view quite a bit on the Fenix 9, though admittedly, half the time I forget to tap the little compass icon to toggle it on. Plus, I don’t tend to stay on the mapping page for very long, since the mapping page on every watch is the fastest way to see just how little battery life you’ll actually get (map pages burn battery life like crazy on every wearable).

Wrap-Up:

Ultimately, the Enduro 4 is one of those Garmin upgrades that really isn’t about appealing to the prior-gen owners. Just like most Apple Watch upgrades aren’t about appealing to people who just bought last year. Instead, it’s primarily targeted at existing Enduro 1 or Enduro 2 owners who would get a big boost in terms of sports features as well as daily life things. And I suppose, for those who simply want the new Fenix 9 features now, versus waiting for Garmin to release those planned updates to the existing Enduro 3 owners.

While some might want even longer battery life, or perhaps a better MIP display, or perhaps changes in solar – the reality is that those are all industry-leading within the category in real-world usage. The Enduro 4 (and Enduro 3 before it) already has the longest GPS battery life out there, even before solar gains are considered, which can push it notably higher. As for the MIP displays, the reality is that there are very few companies making these panels, and they have very little reason to innovate in an area that continues to see dwindling unit volume. Certainly, I’d love to see a more readable MIP display in dimmer conditions, but I have a feeling that’s not happening anytime soon. Especially as AMOLED watch unit overall battery life continues to climb closer and closer to MIP display units.

In any event, assuming you’re choosing a MIP display unit, between the Garmin Enduro 4 vs Enduro 3 vs Fenix 9, I think the question you ask yourself is relatively simple: Do you care about scuba diving, microphone/speaker features, LTE, Satellite Communications, or a smaller 43/47mm unit? If the answer to all of those is ‘Nah’, then the Enduro is the clear winner. If you go for the Enduro 4, you’ll save yourself $200 over the Fenix 9 Solar unit priced at $1,099+. If you want to save a bit, you could pick up the Enduro 3 at a bit cheaper today, knowing it’ll get virtually all those new Enduro 4 software features in a few months or so. What the future in a year or two brings, I’ve got no idea (and I suspect Garmin hasn’t decided yet either).

In any case, hopefully all the above was useful in helping you decide.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: More Wild Horses Than Cars
entry.content:
Thirty riders, eighty-eight miles, and the quiet fall backcountry of Routt County. Rapha x Moots Brevet, a fall gravel ride out of Steamboat Springs, Colorado.

Words by Richard Jara · Photos by Keegan Ashton, Nate Bradley


Friday

The factory is winding down on a Friday evening. The welding torches are off, and tubing sits racked along the walls in the miter shop. Evening light shines through settling into the corners. On the Friday before the Brevet, the shop floor filled with riders who had driven in, most of them from Boulder and the Front Range. We started the night with a tour, a look into the process behind a handbuilt titanium gravel bike, and a look back at Moots' history as we celebrate our 45th anniversary. Then we shared food and drinks to fuel up for Saturday's ride.

A brevet isn't a race. No clock, no podium, no free socks. There's the route, the people on it with you, and the experience shared after a hard day.

This day asked a lot.

Saturday morning. Thirty riders gather outside the Moots factory for the start.


The Climb

Wolf Mountain to Sand Mountain. The loop strings together some of our favorite roads and surfaces, from champagne gravel to rocky, rooted two-track over the divide.

The Route · 87.6 mi · 8,416 ft of climbing

Ride it yourself: Wolf Mountain x Sand Mountain on Ride with GPS →

The loop leaves the valley quickly, turning onto dirt county roads and winding through Mystic to the base of Wolf Mountain. If you weren't committed to the full route this was your chance to cut the route shorter. Long fence lines, grazing cows, and the quiet chill of morning. Golden, sunburnt hills in every direction, with dark pines along the high ridges, and off to the north sits the watershed divide we'd be crossing hours later. Recent rains had packed the dirt firm. We couldn't have asked for a better window.

More wild horses than cars. Somewhere in California Park, Routt National Forest

The climbing doesn't let up. It builds steadily through the first half, mile after mile, until the high point near mile fifty. By then the group had strung out across the route.

Nate Bradley putting the new Routt through its paces. Meet the new Routt →


Sand Mountain

The descent off Sand Mountain was, in Torin Lackmann's words, "chonky" loose, rocky, and a little above everyone's comfort zone. At the bottom, a pop-up aid station was waiting. Huge thanks to Gina, Keegan, and Indy for being there with food, water, and good spirits for a lot of tired souls.

Food, water, and good spirits at the bottom of Sand Mountain.


Home

From there, thirty miles and about 2,000 feet of climbing stood between us and the finish, most of it trending downhill. After Sand Mountain, the final stretch felt well earned, smooth champagne gravel over long, rolling hills, with the valley and Steamboat slowly coming back into view.

"The absolute fall ride of my dreams. Has to be my favorite single day out of the year. So pretty. So fun. So flowy. All. Time."

— Torin Lackmann, Rapha Boulder

Thirty riders rolled out that morning. They rolled back in dusty, cooked, and grinning. Post-ride beers waiting.

"Although there were a couple of hard, dark moments, everyone seemed to have an amazing ride. One rider told us back at the shop that afternoon it was the best gravel ride he'd ever done, hands down. We're truly lucky to have terrain like this right outside our front door. It validates why we make the bikes we do."

— Nate Bradley, Moots

We build bikes like the new Routt for days like this. Long days, rough roads, and every side of the map to explore.

Thanks to Rapha Boulder for making the trip to our corner of Colorado and making the roads we know by heart feel new again, and to all thirty of you for riding them with us.

Want to ride it yourself? Here's the route.

See you out there.

entry.title: One of One: The Vamoots CRD × Mavic x Campagnolo
entry.content:
Every so often a build comes along that only happens once. This is one of those.

When we were deciding what special project to bring to MADE 2026 in Portland, we kept landing on the same answer. Road. So that is what we built: a one-of-one Vamoots CRD, painted for this collaboration, built with Mavic and Campagnolo. It debuted at the show, and it is the only one we will make.

Handcrafted in Steamboat Springs, the way we have always done it since 1981.

The story

We have been welding titanium by hand in Steamboat for decades. Mavic has been building wheels for over a century. Campagnolo has been shaping road groupsets in Italy for generations. This bike puts all three on one frame, shaping the purest expression of the craft. Road.

The finish is where this one lives. A soft sea-foam green over the front triangle fades to white, with pinstripe detailing running through it. Get the light on it right and the paint stops behaving like paint. Fine flake sits suspended in the clear coat, and for a second, the right light catches it like the surface is still wet. The matching Moots seat post leaves a band of raw titanium exposed, and the Enve one-piece cockpit and fork are painted to match. Chris King's Jade finish on the headset, hubs, and lockrings ties it all together. The Jade Chris King surface is matte, but the color isn't flat, it shifts slightly depending on the light and the angle you're looking from. No two glances land the same. We designed the finish in-house for this frame, one of one.

The build

The Vamoots CRD sits at the top of our road line. It starts with our double-butted RSL titanium tubeset and runs a fully integrated cockpit, so the lines stay clean and the cables stay out of sight.

  • Frame: Vamoots CRD, 54cm, RSL double-butted titanium tubeset
  • Wheels: Mavic Comete 55/65
  • Groupset: Campagnolo Super Record 13, 2x13, 55/39T, 11-36
  • Finish: one-off MADE 2026 custom paint
  • Highlights: 3D-printed dropouts, Fully integrated, T47 bottom bracket, 32c tire clearance

See the full spec

The only one

Give us a blank canvas and one bike to make, and this is the result. Our best road platform, the best parts our partners build, and a finish that exists exactly once. An ode to the road, from a shop that has always loved it. Made to last.

There is only one, and this is it. The bike you have been looking at is the one for sale. See the full build and make it yours.

More from MADE 2026

The Vamoots CRD wasn't the only thing we brought to Portland. If you missed the show, here's the rest of what was on the floor:

  • The limited-edition "Phase" finish on the new Womble — the etched-and-anodized fade that ended up stealing the show. The Radavist has the finish story and a full gallery.
  • The new Routt — our reworked gravel platform, built around bigger rubber and a 3D-printed yoke, shown as a prototype. More to come soon. BIKEPACKING walked through it.
  • The new all road - one bike for smooth road, broken pavement, and the gravel shortcut, with clearance up to 42c. Shown a a prototype, more to come.
  • The 32" prototypes — two big-wheel hardtails we're still testing, including the Scrambler 32. Also in BIKEPACKING's builder rundown.

The conversations, the rides, the stoke, that's why we do this. Events like MADE are never just about the bikes, they're about the people who show up for them. Thank you for being a part of it.

We'll be back on the road later this year. Find us at Bespoked Japan in Osaka, October 23 to 25, and Rouleur Live in London this November.

Until next time.

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: KELSEY HUTCHINSON
entry.content:
From Fashion to Frames

Kelsey’s path to Moots began far from a welding bench. After stepping away from a career in fashion journalism in New York City, she returned to her hometown of Omaha, Nebraska, looking for something more hands-on. A job at a local bike and coffee shop sparked a growing interest in cycling, but everything changed after visiting Co-Motion Cycles in Oregon. Watching a frame being welded made the direction clear. Two days later, she quit her classes and enrolled in welding school with one goal in mind: to build bicycle frames.

Betting on the Craft

Welding school in the Midwest focused on structural welding, not bikes. The idea of becoming a framebuilder earned skeptical looks and advice about taking a long, traditional path. Moots saw her focus and commitment and hired her before she even graduated.

“I went to welding school with the sole purpose of building bicycle frames.”

The Reality of Building a Moots

While Moots bikes travel the world, Kelsey works within an intentionally small team of makers behind the scenes. Every frame is built by hand, with pride taken in each step of the process and the details that define a Moots.

Challenges and Wins

Most bike welds are smooth curves, which makes the occasional straight-line weld surprisingly difficult. For Kelsey, welding binders onto steerer blanks can be the most challenging. The most satisfying moments come when everything lines up, especially nailing the drive-side front triangle welds.

No Compromises

Kelsey credits much of her growth to the people around her. Teammates who have been welding for years continue to push her to refine her craft and show up striving for that extra one percent. For her, “No Compromises” means honoring the trust riders place in Moots by delivering nothing short of perfect.

Forever Bikes

Bikes are memory makers. Even if a bike eventually changes hands, the rides, adventures, and everyday moments tied to it stay with the rider. Knowing she had a hand in creating something that meaningful is what keeps Kelsey invested in every weld.

Why Titanium

Steel is fine. Aluminum is less forgiving. Titanium is different. Smooth, precise, and endlessly satisfying to weld, it’s the material that keeps her inspired at the bench.

Life Beyond the Bench

Kelsey rides a Routt 45, RCS, Womble, and a Routt CRD. Outside the shop, she stays active year-round with workouts, dance classes, boot packing with her dogs in the winter, and riding or gardening when the snow melts. Her go-to coffee is a light roast with a splash of cream, unless she’s feeling sassy, then it’s a cortado. While others tune into music, she listens to true crime podcasts.

 

The People

Ask Kelsey her favorite part of Moots, and the answer is simple: the people. The factory feels like family, and that sense of trust runs deep. Being asked by a coworker to weld their frame is still one of the highest honors.

Dream Ride

If she could take any Moots anywhere, she knows exactly where she’d go. Spain, on two wheels, is high on the list.

entry.title: San Francisco Bay Area Loop by Thomas Woodson
entry.content:
The San Francisco Bay Area, despite its massive population, holds an equally massive amount of protected land: networks of multi-use trails and campgrounds stitched throughout. You trade remoteness for convenience, but this kind of variety is something I love to fold into my bikepacking goals. Plentiful food, quality sleep, hard-charging downhills—elements worth remembering the next time you’re really out there and feeling a bit thrashed.

My introduction to the area was the SF Peninsula Traverse, a route I used to start a weeklong ride from San Francisco Airport to Los Angeles Airport in 2019. In 2024, Adam Sklar showed me around some of the Marin and Fairfax classics. I’ve been fascinated by the sheer number of options ever since, to the point that my Gaia GPS maps are now borderline too cluttered to navigate.

Looking for ways to combine the SF Peninsula Traverse with the Bay Area Triple Crossover led us to Bikepack the Bay—a 265-mile, +27,000ft route that we trimmed slightly to fit more comfortably into a three-day window with limited December daylight.

Day 1 covered 64 miles and +5,600ft from Sklar’s shop in the Mission District, following the SF Peninsula Traverse through Half Moon Bay, climbing into the redwoods (at night), and dropping into a Palo Alto hotel. The route starts urban, slowly dissolving into crumbling abandoned roads through the hills, coastline bike paths, and finally a lush, pine-needle climb that’s absolutely grueling. From Skyline Road, the Kings Mountain Road descent—ridden in the dark—was the best road descent of my life. Dynamo-illuminated reflectors twisted through the redwoods like the ultimate video game.

Day 2 began with a long bridge and shoreline crossing, then followed nearly the entire skyline from Fremont to Richmond along the Bay Area Ridge Trail (decently signed).  77 miles and +7,700ft. Spending the entire day on bike paths, wide dirt roads, and ripping singletrack was hard to believe given the proximity to millions of people. Fifty-two-tooth cassettes and the absence of camping gear were especially welcome for just how steep every climb was on this stretch.

Day 3 opened with another bridge traverse and 67 miles of +7,300ft along ridge top fire roads to Lagunitas—the only resupply point—before a final push along Bolinas Ridge, around Tam, and across the Golden Gate back into San Francisco. Once again, a full day without really touching a road. We skipped the Headlands trails as sunset approached, but there are plenty of options to explore there.

The varied, ever-changing terrain kept us engaged. The urban offered a reprieve from the steeps; the steeps, a reprieve from the urban. Staying in cheap hotels felt like a luxury—less luggage, more riding. Kyle is typically the route master when we’re out together, but I believe I showed him some things to change his perspectives this time around. The Bay Area is about to be one of our winter classics.

Tips
– Navigation is constant. A head unit is essential, and having the tracks on your phone as backup is smart. Trail closures around the Baylands in Palo Alto before the bridge crossing added a few miles of backtracking
– The Richmond Bridge closes the bike lane during the week but offers a free shuttle bus in its place. If you want to ride it, check schedules and plan a weekend crossing
– Keeping a variety of Bay Area routes saved allows for easy on-the-fly modifications or side quests
– SFO Airport offers luggage storage and a bike stand if you want to start and finish the loop there

Incredible resources:
SF Peninsula Traverse – https://bikepacking.com/routes/sf-peninsula-traverse/
Bay Area Triple Crossover – https://bikepacking.com/routes/bay-area-triple-crossover/
Bay Area Ridge Trail – https://ridgetrail.org/
Bikepack the Bay – https://www.bikepackthebay.com/

--- 

Thomas Woodson is a Colorado-based photographer and Moots ambassador known for capturing long days, quiet moments, and the kind of riding that rewards curiosity over convenience. He currently rides a dropbar MXC in our Groundswell finish, a setup well suited to the mixed terrain and exploratory routes that shape his work.

entry.title: Winter Desert Miles
entry.content:
When the temperatures drop and the mountains start to get capped with snow, many of us in the mountains start looking south. As winter settles into the high country and riding up high fades, the desert opens up. Cooler days, fewer crowds, and long stretches of quiet make late fall and early winter the right time to ride White Rim. It’s not about speed or numbers—it’s about choosing the season, committing to the miles, and finding space before winter fully takes hold. Richard takes us on his adventure on the White Rim outside of the famed Moab, Utah. 

I just got back from eight days in the desert.

Already checking the weather for the next warm window, planning how I’m going to keep riding through winter, something I’ve always abandoned for skiing. Living in the mountains, you share an unspoken bond with winter. It’s a fortunate place with easy access to snow and the outdoors. I’ve skied resort and earned my uphill turns for the last nine years, but lately the chairlift scene feels played out. So when opening weekend and the first storm of the year rolled through, I did the opposite and headed west, away from the noise. Offseason in Moab.

Bike choice: Routt CRD. 34mm road slicks mounted. 44mm Mezcals in the truck for when dirt was good

One bike. Keep it simple. 

Day one: blue sky above the red rock canyons, fresh snow on the La Sals. No wind, just stillness in the cold desert air. Cold start that never really warmed up, but I was out there riding, and that was the plan. River Road to Castle Valley, then out and back to Arches National Park. One hundred scenic miles, and 7k. Easily one of the best road rides in the country. Had to bail into the truck near the end, blast the heaters, and warm up. Then back outside to finish it. Glad I did. 

I fell into a rhythm for the next three days. Wake up, coffee, pick a direction, go ride, try not to freeze. Hit all the Moab road classics: 313 out to Island in the Sky, Potash Road, the Canyon Path, Arches, Upper Colorado River Scenic Byway to Dewey Bridge. Missed the window for La Sal Mountain Loop Road, but that was okay. 

The views in the Moab desert are magnificent, whether you're on pavement or deep in the desert. I was chasing another route. By the end of the week, after the cold front cleared, it became clear that conditions in Canyonlands would be dry enough. Saturday would be the day. Forecast in the 50s. White Rim.

White Rim is a one-hundred-mile route through the Island in the Sky district of Canyonlands National Park. First rode it in December 2019, but I keep coming back to check in. It's become a benchmark. A testing ground. An escape. Just hard enough. Just remote enough. But this wasn't about PRs or pushing numbers. This was about chasing desert miles and the low winter sun. About being out there and just riding.

Texted Andrew on Friday. “White Rim tomorrow?”

“Yeah, I'm in.”

Quick logistics: 8am start, Mineral Bottom/313 intersection, counter-clockwise. Day permits sorted. Self-supported, everything we needed on the bikes. Keep it simple.  Andrew runs a custom bikepacking gear company with his wife Katie, out of an off-grid workshop at the foot of the La Sal Mountains. We first connected on the Colorado Trail back in 2019. It's always good to reconnect with racing friends, and to ride with someone who gets the appeal of long days, minimal setups, and backcountry routes. I’ve taken a lot of inspiration from the way Andrew approaches cycling and racing. Most of the ride was a conversation about gear, bikes, and what’s next on the list. By then, we had already approached the final climb up Schafer Trail, the sun had gone down, and we rolled the final 8ish miles by headlamp. A full day on the pedals, no major mechanical issues, and good conditions. Hard to ask for more.  

On the way back to the mountains, I stopped and camped on 18rd in Fruita, spun the legs out once more around the Colorado National Monument, another Colorado classic. Back to winter, for now. 

https://www.strava.com/athletes/6042499

 - Richard

entry.title: MEET THE MAKER: ERIC HINDES
entry.content:
25 Years of Craft, Curiosity, and Getting It Right

Some people find their way to bike building through formal paths. Others through obsession. For Eric Hindes, it started at home and it stuck.

Eric has been part of the Moots team for 25 years. Today, he programs and runs multiple CNC machines, helps shape how we manufacture frames and components in-house, and carries decades of institutional knowledge across the production floor. But like many great bike builders, his story starts long before his first day at Moots.

A Family Affair and a Pile of Magazines

Eric’s entry into bikes came courtesy of his dad. Mountain biking was new, exciting, and everywhere in the pages of Fat Tire Flyer, Mountain Bike, Dirt Rag, and Bike.
